## Abstract

This thesis examines how the parliamentary representation of smaller parties is affected by the transition from Hagenbach-Bischoff to Double Pukelsheim. To do so, all 31 available cantonal parliamentary elections for the eight transition cantons between 2007 and 2026 are analyzed. The smaller parties group combines all electoral lists and parties which received less than 10% of the total votes in the analyzed area. To make this comparison, the official results under Double Pukelsheim are taken and the counterfactual seat allocation under Hagenbach-Bischoff is computed. In addition are the former cantonal electoral laws included and the electoral units, observed votes, seat totals and reported list structures are held constant. 

The main finding is that across all 31 elections, the smaller parties aggregately receive a seat-share 7.6 percentage points higher under Double Pukelsheim than under the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff. An aggregate gain for the smaller parties occurs in 30 of 31 elections. Further is the observed gain persistent to alternative smaller-party thresholds, across successive elections and to the omission of individual cantons. While analyses regarding the pre-reform district magnitude or explicit electoral thresholds, reveal no consistent relationship, respectively are sensitive to the inclusion of individual cantons.

The persistent mechanical seat-share gain for smaller parties observed here indicates the reduction of the prior representational disadvantage under the Double Pukelsheim system. Behavioural responses to the reform remain outside the scope of the analysis.

## Introduction
On the 18th December of 2002 the Swiss Federal Supreme Court (FSC) came to a conclusion, which disrupted the Swiss Electoral System. In BGE 129 I 185 the FSC criticized that in the elections for the Council of the City of Zurich, the thresholds in some districts were up to 34% high. Furthermore varied the thresholds heavily across the districts. Consequently, votes did not have equal effect, which undermined the electoral equality included in Art. 8 (Equality before the law) and Art. 34 (political rights) of the Federal Constitution. Based on this criticism the court decided that the City of Zurich had to implement corrective measures, but let the city choose the way of reform (BGE 129 I 185 E. 7.3, E. 7.6.2–7.6.3 and E. 8.3.2; Schweizerische Eidgenossenschaft, 1999, Arts. 8 and 34). The Government of the Canton of Zurich decided to keep the constituency structure and  instead commissioned the German mathematician Friedrich Pukelsheim to develop a comprehensive and at the same time minimally invasive solution for the problem. Eventually Pukelsheim came up with a method called "biproportional divisor method with standard rounding" which is today often simply called "Double Pukelsheim" or "Biproportional apportionment". (Regierungsrat des Kantons Zürich, 2014, pp. 3–4; Lüscher, 2024, pp. 9-10)

The distinguishing feature of the Pukelsheim Proporz compared with Hagenbach-Bischoff, is the so called upper-apportionment. It artificially creates a single electoral district for the initial allocation of the parliamentary seats to the parties or list groups. Through this mechanism, the difference between seat and vote shares gets minimized and with that also the effective threshold for parties to enter the parliament. (Lüscher, 2023, p. 575) This mechanism and the lowered threshold make the reform especially relevant for the representation of smaller parties, since votes that would previously have been ineffective in small constituencies can now contribute to a seat gain at the cantonal level. Sandro Lüscher illustrates this mechanical effect with the case of the Schwyz Kantonsrat election in 2016. In that election, did the Green Liberal Party receive three seats, whereas under the old HB system it would have received none (Lüscher, 2025, p. 1-3).

Since Zurich first used the system in 2007, eight further cantons have applied it: Schaffhausen (2008), Aargau (2009), Nidwalden (2014), Zug (2014), Schwyz (2016) , Valais (2017) , Uri (2020) and Graubünden (2022). In 2025 also the voters from Basel-Landschaft decided to implement the biproportional apportionment from 2027 on (Lüscher , 2024, p.17 ; Kanton Basel-Landschaft, 2025a, p.7 ; Kanton Basel-Landschaft, 2025b). While nine of the swiss cantons have already implemented the DP system, in Thurgau, Lucerne and St.Gallen, the application is currently under debate (Grosser Rat des Kantons Thurgau, n.d.; Regierungsrat des Kantons Luzern, 2026, pp. 19–20 ; Initiativkomitee «Damit jede Stimme zählt», n.d.).

The number of cantons who have already implemented the system or are debating about doing so suggests that the decision by the FSC had a substantial impact on how Swiss citizens elect their regional parliaments today. It seems that the Double Pukelsheim through its wide implementation across cantons is a success story. Since the first election under Double Pukelsheim in Zurich in 2007, the system has been used in 33 cantonal parliamentary elections.^[The 33 elections comprise Zurich (2007, 2011, 2015, 2019, and 2023; Amt für Statistik und Daten Kanton Zürich, 2026); Schaffhausen (2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024; Kanton Schaffhausen, n.d.; Staatskanzlei Kanton Schaffhausen, 2020, 2024); Aargau (2009, 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024; Departement für Finanzen und Ressourcen des Kantons Aargau, 2009; Regierungsrat des Kantons Aargau, 2013; Statistisches Amt Kanton Aargau, n.d.); Nidwalden (2014, 2018, 2022, and 2026; Staatskanzlei Nidwalden, 2014, 2018, 2022, 2026); Zug (2014, 2018, 2022, and 2026; Kanton Zug, 2022a, 2022b, 2022c, 2026); Schwyz (2016, 2020, and 2024; Staatskanzlei Kanton Schwyz, 2016, 2020, 2024); Valais (2017, 2021, and 2025; Kanton Wallis, 2016, 2020, 2024; Staat Wallis, 2017); Uri (2020 and 2024; Standeskanzlei Uri, 2024a, 2024b); and Graubünden (2022 and 2026; Kanton Graubünden, 2022, 2026).] 

Taken together, this number of elections and almost 20 years of experience provide a reason to evaluate the impact of the reform, especially on smaller parties. How much has the reform changed smaller' parties seat shares and how large is the actual difference in seat allocation between the Hagenbach-Bischoff and Double Pukelsheim systems? Are there other major differences, for example based on the pre-reform district sizes and how do smaller parties' seat shares evolve across successive elections?

Existing research primarily examines Double Pukelsheim in legal, normative, or system-level terms. A few studies also conduct counterfactual comparisons, but these cover either individual elections or only one election per canton (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, pp. 1590–1592; Leuzinger, 2018, p. 42; Lüscher, 2024, p. 13). Although their results indicate that smaller parties can benefit from Double Pukelsheim, the magnitude and consistency of this mechanical allocation difference across successive elections remain less systematically examined.

This thesis addresses this gap by applying a consistent Hagenbach–Bischoff counterfactual to 31 elections in eight transition cantons. Two Graubünden elections are presented as contextual comparisons but excluded from the main transition estimate. Holding the observed post-reform votes and list structure constant, the analysis measures the difference in the share of seats won by smaller electoral lists and examines variation across institutional settings and successive elections.

## Theory and Literature Review

### Institutional and Theoretical Background

This chapter provides the institutional and theoretical background for analyzing the transition from Hagenbach-Bischoff to Double Pukelsheim and reviews the relevant literature. It first outlines the historical development of electoral systems in Switzerland and then explains the functioning and limitations of the Hagenbach-Bischoff and Double Pukelsheim methods. It subsequently examines the adoption and canton-specific implementation of Double Pukelsheim. Finally, the literature review situates this thesis within previous research before the expected effects of the transition are derived.

#### Historical Development

Until the late nineteenth century Swiss voters elected their regional parliaments only under majority voting. In a majority voting system, the candidates or parties who receive the relative or absolute majority receive the mandates, which leads to a systematic favouring of the dominant parties. Over time, this inequality led to dissatisfaction among smaller parties. Subsequently, these demanded a change to a proportional electoral system. The calls for change, led to that most of the cantons' Grand Councils as well as the National Council were later elected with the Hagenbach-Bischoff or another proportional system. In the beginning of the 21st century, the cantons of Graubünden and Appenzell Innerrhoden were the only ones to still elect their parliaments with the majority system. (Gilg, 2014, “Mehrheits- und Verhältniswahl” section ; Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 2) Nowadays the canton Appenzell Innerrhoden is the only remaining canton voting the Grand Council by majority voting (Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p. 18). It can therefore be said, that proportional systems have become the dominating electoral systems for cantonal parliaments in Switzerland. 

In the last 20 years the prior dominance of the Hagenbach-Bischoff system has been demolished by the wide implementation of the Pukelsheim Algorithm. As of 2025, eleven cantons apply the parliamentary seats with Hagenbach-Bischoff and ten cantons with the DP, Glarus and Basel-Stadt use the Sainte-Laguë method, Ticino and Vaud use the Hare/Niemeyer method and Appenzell Innerrhoden majority voting (Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p.18). Both Hare/Niemeyer and Sainte-Laguë are generally associated with a higher proportionality than the HB system, therefore this might partly explain why none of the cantons using these two PR-Systems have adopted the Double Pukelsheim system (Bundeskanzlei, 2025, pp. 22; Deutscher Bundestag, 2007, p.9). This means that of the nine cantons analyzed here, eight previously mainly used Hagenbach-Bischoff. The special cases are Graubünden, Zug and Uri, where majority voting had been used canton-wide respectively in at least one municipiality. (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, Table 1; BGE 136 I 376 E. 5.1 ; Standeskanzlei Uri, 2020, p. 1; Statistisches Amt des Kantons Zürich, 2011, p. 286; Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 2007, p. 6; Regierungsrat des Kantons Aargau, 2007, p. 18). 

#### The Hagenbach-Bischoff Method {#sec-hb-method}

To be able to comprehend later the differences between the HB and the DP Method one has to understand the allocation under the priorly used Hagenbach-Bischoff system. 

Under Hagenbach-Bischoff, seats are allocated separately in each constituency. Let $M$ denote the number of mandates in the constituency, $v_i$ the votes for an eligible list $i$, $V$ the total number of valid list votes of all lists in the constituency used to calculate the distribution number and $D$ the distribution number for the smallest integer strictly greater than $V/(M+1)$. In the first allocation, each list receives the integer part of its votes divided by $D$. (Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p. 41)

$$
D = \left\lfloor \frac{V}{M + 1} \right\rfloor + 1, \qquad s_i = \left\lfloor \frac{v_i}{D} \right\rfloor.
$$

If the first allocation leaves seats unassigned, the remaining seats are awarded one at a time. For each list, its votes are divided by the number of seats it currently holds plus one. The list with the highest quotient receives the next seat, its quotient $h_i$ and the allocated seats $s_i$ are then recalculated, and the process continues until all $M$ seats have been filled:

$$
h_i = \frac{v_i}{s_i + 1}.
$$

It should be noted, that the HB system calculation produces the same allocation as the D'Hondt divisor method with downward rounding (Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p. 41). Furthermore there are factors, like list alliances, explicit electoral thresholds, and rules for resolving equal quotients which depend on the electoral law of the corresponding canton. The counterfactual in this thesis applies the relevant former cantonal rules within each constituency, as detailed in @sec-assumptions-scope .

The central weakness of the traditional cantonal application of Hagenbach–Bischoff arises from applying the formula separately across constituencies which often have few seats. Small district magnitudes create high natural thresholds, meaning that votes for smaller parties may fail to contribute to a seat. This might hinder equality of electoral success and systematically disadvantage smaller parties. As shown in the later section on the adoption of Double Pukelsheim, these inequalities were central to the legal and political debates that led several cantons to adopt Double Pukelsheim. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, pp. 507-508, 521; BGE 129 I 185 E. 7.1.1 and E. 7.6.2)

#### The Double Pukelsheim Method

Based on the weaknesses of the Hagenbach-Bischoff Method and the FSC decision, the canton of Zurich commissioned the mathematician Friedrich Pukelsheim to develop a new method (Lüscher, 2024, p.10). The following section explores its mechanism and differences to the Hagenbach-Bischoff method.

Based on Articles 8 and 34 of the Federal Constitution, there are three dimensions of electoral equality, which have to be followed. These are the principle of equal voting value, equality of voting power  and equality of electoral success. The equal voting value ensures that each voter within an electoral district gets allocated the identical number of votes. The second principle requires the population represented per seat to be approximately equal across electoral districts. Thirdly the equality of electoral success should assure, that all votes contribute equally to the election and that as many votes as possible are included in the allocation of the mandates. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, pp. 506-507) Districts with fewer than nine seats have a natural quorum above 10%, making it difficult for smaller parties to enter the seat allocation in that district. The FSC treats 10% as a target for natural quorums when redesigning an electoral system. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 505; BGE 131 I 74 E. 5.2–5.4) For the traditional application of Hagenbach–Bischoff, the main difficulty is, that small districts contradict the 10% target. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 508; BGE 129 I 185 E. 7.1.1 and E. 7.6.2)

To approach this issue, the Double Pukelsheim uses an upper and a lower apportionment (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p.513). 

- **Upper Apportionment** To bypass the natural quorums, in the upper apportionment, the whole canton is seen as one single district. Seats are allocated to parties in proportion to their cantonal vote shares. To achieve this, the votes from the district-level have to be summarized on a cantonal level. Because of the different district magnitudes, voters receive a different amount of votes. Therefore, the number of votes has to be translated to a cantonal level. This is done by dividing the number of party votes per constituency by the respective number of seats. The resulting quotient gets rounded to the nearest integer and represents the voter equivalents. The rounded quotients, can then be summed across all districts and divided by the cantonal divisor to get each party's total seats. The divisor itself is set by an official authority, in Zurich for example, it's the Department of Justice and Home Affairs. The divisor needs to be set so, that exactly as many seats can be allocated as there are available. The number of seats which result per party, are rounded again to the next number to receive the upper apportionment seat entitlement. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p.1584-1585 ; Kanton Zürich, 2003, § 10 and 103)

- **Lower Apportionment** This part of the apportionment process, assigns each party's cantonwide seats from the upper apportionment to its district lists while preserving each district's predetermined seat total. First, the party votes in each district are divided by the corresponding district divisor. The divisor is chosen so that the rounded results add up to the district's seats (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1585). These initial allocations may not match the parties' cantonwide entitlements. For example in the 2011 Zurich election this ocurred, where the SVP would have received 55 seats instead of the 54 assigned in the upper apportionment . To correct such differences, every district list of a party is divided by the same additional list group divisor. A divisor above one reduces the party's unrounded quotients and can remove seats while a divisor below one can add seats. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1586) The arising effect can be illustrated with a hypothetical numerical example based on the 2011 seat mismatch for the SVP. Now it could be that the SVP list in District Y would have a quotient after division by the district divisor of 2.51. With the standard rounding, the SVP would receive three seats in this district. Given that the SVP quotient is closest to downrounding in that district, one would choose a number which rounds the quotient down to two seats e.g. with $2.51/1.01 \approx 2.49$. Through that the mismatch would be resolved, but the change in District Y might cause, that the district gets allocated one seat too few. The party and district divisors are then adjusted in turn until every party receives its cantonwide entitlement and every district retains its fixed number of seats. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1586)

To summarize, the upper apportionment in the Double Pukelsheim system reduces inequalities in electoral success caused by the high natural thresholds of small constituencies under the previous district-by-district Hagenbach-Bischoff system. It does so by pooling parties' votes across the canton before seats are assigned to constituencies. This is also the main improvement of DP regarding the three dimensions of electoral equality in contrast to Hagenbach-Bischoff. 

##### Trade-offs and Criticisms

Like every proportional system, also the Double Pukelsheim system has flaws for which it gets criticized. One of the main weaknesses of the biproportional apportionment compared to the HB System is its complexity. It gets mentioned throughout, that the system is relatively difficult to understand and compute. (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 19 ; Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p.24 ; Lüscher, 2024, p.20) Lüscher though mentions, that the list alliances used under Hagenbach-Bischoff also led to a high complexity situation. This especially since, before an election it was impossible to estimate, which party would profit from the alliance. (Lüscher, 2024, p.20) Another main point of criticism is the so called "discordant seat allocations". They describe the phenomenon when within a district a party gets allocated more seats than another party with more votes in that district. This phenomena can appear through the lower apportionment process and the dual role of the system to achieve proportionality both on cantonal and district-level. The emerging situation, can cause confusion and frustration especially within the party which received more votes in that specific constituency. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 519) Not only for the parties themselves can it be irritating, but also for the voters, this especially since in Switzerland elections often contain a personal vote component. A reaction to this flaw of the DP-System, was that the cantons of Zug, Schaffhausen and Graubünden implemented a majority clause, which aims to ensure that the strongest list in the corresponding constituency receives at least one seat. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 21) Friedrich Pukelsheim was already aware of the issue in 2004 and pointed out that the majority requirement can in rare ocassions be not fulfilled and subsequently pointed out the usage of a majority clause. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, p. 520) Another issue of the system, is that different turnout levels and different proportions of residents who are eligible to vote in the constituencies can determine the allocated mandates of other constituencies. To illustrate this, Lüscher provides an example: There are three districts with the same size and number of mandates, but while District 1 produces 50% of all votes, District 2 and 3 only produce each 25%. Through this District 1 determines 50% of the canton-wide party result, while only having 33.3% of the mandates. Subsequently this leads to under- and overrepresentation in the corresponding districts. (Lüscher, 2023, pp. 578-579) One other point which was often discussed to be a possible weakness of the Double Pukelsheim, is a possible Party System Fragmentation. For example both reports of the Swiss Federal Chancellery in 2013 and 2025 mention it and introduce the usage of explicit thresholds to prevent it. (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p.18 ; Bundeskanzlei, 2025, p. 24) Despite these concerns, Sandro Lüscher came to the perception, that the general trend of a rising amount of parties in Swiss cantonal parliaments, is unrelated to the implementation of the Double Pukelsheim. He then also mentioned, that the inexistency of an effect, might come from that several cantons have implemented thresholds. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 135) Therefore it can't be conclusively stated, whether the reform would have had an impact on party system fragmentation without the implementation of thresholds or not. 

Taken together, these criticisms illustrate the central trade-offs of Double Pukelsheim. Although the system improves canton-wide proportionality and reduces the number of ineffective votes, it does so at the cost of greater complexity and potentially counterintuitive outcomes at the constituency level. Electoral thresholds can mitigate discordant seat allocations and party-system fragmentation, but may simultaneously weaken proportionality. The system therefore does not eliminate electoral distortions entirely.

#### The Adoption of Double Pukelsheim in Swiss Cantons {#sec-adoption}
As outlined in the section Historical Development, did the Double Pukelsheim gain popularity after its initial implementation in Zurich. The form, reason, and circumstances under which its applied, though vary from canton to canton. The subsequent table provides an overview of the different ways of implementation across the cantons.

| **Canton** | **First election under DP** | **Main reform driver** | **Explicit electoral thresholds** |
|:---|:---:|:---|:---|
| Zurich | 2007 | Reaction to the FSC ruling for the City of Zurich, since the canton faced similar issues | 5% district-level (2007-2019), 5% district-level or 3% cantonal-level (2023-) |
| Schaffhausen | 2008 | Parliament was downsized, subsequently reforms were needed, In view of the FSC judgements in Zurich and Aargau, Double Pukelsheim was chosen | None |
| Aargau | 2009 | Parliament was downsized, no Action regarding electoral equality was taken, the FSC ruled for change and followingly the implementation of DP was decided | None (2009), 5% district-level or 3% cantonal-level (2012-) |
| Nidwalden | 2014 | Voters appeal at cantonal court and later at FSC, FSC decided in favour of the appeal, the DP system was favoured as a solution and implemented | None |
| Zug | 2014 | Voters and parties appeal at the FSC, Court agrees on the main point, the DP system is favoured and implemented | 5% district-level or 3% cantonal-level |
| Schwyz | 2016 | Voters appeal at the FSC based on the new constitution and its districts, FSC agreed partly, multiple options were explored, finally the DP-system was implemented. | 1% cantonal-level |
| Valais | 2017 | FSC appeal in 2004 was rejected, a second appeal was approved by the FSC, subsequently implementation of DP was done via a temporary decree because of lacking electorate approval, later the system was officially incorporated | 8% sub-district-level |
| Uri | 2020 | Appeal at the FSC was partially upheld, subsequently Double Pukelsheim was implemented for municipalities with at least five seats | None |

| Basel-Landschaft | 2027 | A single parliamentarian advocated for the Double Pukelsheim over multiple years, subsequently the implementation was proposed and approved by Parliament and voters | 5% district-level or 3% cantonal-level |

To summarize, in 8 of 10 reform cantons, a raised complaint at the FSC led to a later reform. Only in the cantons of Schaffhausen and Basel-Landschaft did the reform process take place without a Federal Supreme Court ruling. Nevertheless the canton of Schaffhausen's decision was directly influenced by the FSC's decisions in Aargau and Zurich. Throughout all complaints, the concern was electoral equality. In seven of them excessively high natural thresholds in proportional constituencies were central. In Graubünden though, the concerns were mainly raised by its use of the majority system for its large districts and the allocation of seats among constituencies. This demonstrates the influence of the 2002 Federal Supreme Court decision regarding Zurich's City Parliament.

Beyond their different paths to reform, the cantons also implemented Double Pukelsheim under substantially different institutional conditions. The number of seats included in the Double Pukelsheim allocation varies from 37 in Uri where the system applies only to four municipalities to 180 in Zurich (Standeskanzlei Uri, 2020, p. 1; Kanton Zürich, 2003, § 88).  Moreover, some cantons introduced explicit local or canton-wide electoral quorums, whereas others did not, potentially limiting smaller parties’ ability to benefit from the more proportional allocation method. These arrangements have also changed over time for example through the later introduction of thresholds or majority clauses while party competition and vote distributions vary between elections. This institutional variation motivates the later exploratory comparisons : Whether smaller parties' seat-share gains differ by the presence of an explicit electoral threshold and across successive elections within the same canton.

### Literature Review

Building on the institutional mechanisms described above, the existing empirical literature generally finds that Double Pukelsheim improves vote–seat proportionality and benefits parties that were disadvantaged by small electoral districts. However, the studies differ in their research designs, geographical coverage, and treatment of counterfactual electoral rules.

Pukelsheim and Schuhmacher provide an early counterfactual comparison based on the 2011 Zurich election. They apply the former Hagenbach–Bischoff method to the observed votes while assuming four hypothetical list alliances based on political orientations and historical alliances. Under this counterfactual, the larger SVP, SP, and FDP receive additional seats, primarily at the expense of smaller parties such as the BDP and Alternative List. Their calculation also indicates considerably greater inequality in the electoral success of votes under Hagenbach–Bischoff. The analysis nevertheless concerns only one election, and its results depend partly on assumptions about which list alliances parties would have formed. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, pp. 1590–1592)

Lüscher conducts a similar comparison for the 2016 Schwyz election. Under his Hagenbach–Bischoff counterfactual, which does not assume any list alliances, the two biggest parties the SVP and CVP would have benefited, whereas the left alliance and the GLP were disadvantaged. Especially extreme is the difference between the three GLP seats under Double Pukelsheim versus zero seats under the counterfactual HB system. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 13) This example illustrates the potentially substantial effect of the allocation rule on an individual smaller party, but it does not establish whether effects of this magnitude occur systematically across cantons and elections.

Leuzinger broadens the comparison by examining the most recent election in each of the seven cantons that had introduced Double Pukelsheim by 2018. His study is the closest precedent for the present analysis because it calculates hypothetical seat distributions for multiple elections under the former cantonal electoral systems. However, its analysis is limited to seven elections and it assumes that the list alliances observed in the final pre-reform election would have persisted. (Leuzinger, 2018a, p. 42) The present thesis does not carry these historical alliances forward. Consequently, the two counterfactual specifications can produce different Hagenbach–Bischoff seat allocations. Consequently there were differences in the distribution of seats between Leuzinger's study and this study for the cantons that previously used list alliances (Leuzinger, 2018b). This illustrates the sensitivity of counterfactual results to assumptions about unobserved alliance formation. Leuzinger also mentions that he observed, that mainly smaller parties profited from the transition and  that around 10% of the mandates mechanically change the party, through the transition (Leuzinger , 2018a, p.42). 

Taken together, the counterfactual calculations by Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, Lüscher, and Leuzinger constitute the closest methodological precedents for the present thesis. They apply a former allocation rule to votes observed under Double Pukelsheim and compare the resulting counterfactual seat distribution with the actual allocation. Their comparisons therefore hold the observed post-reform vote distribution constant and only isolate the difference produced by the allocation rules.

The interpretation of this difference can be clarified using Fiva and Folke's framework for separating the mechanical and psychological effects of electoral reform. Fiva and Folke examined a reform of Norwegian municipal elections, that replaced D’Hondt with modified Sainte-Laguë. (Fiva & Folke, 2016 , p.266) Their principal estimate of the mechanical reform effect compares the actual pre-reform allocation with a counterfactual application of the new formula to the same pre-reform votes. They also apply the former and new formulas to the same post-reform votes to examine how behavioral responses may alter the magnitude of the mechanical effect. (Fiva & Folke, 2016, pp. 270–272) The Swiss studies described above, and the present thesis, follow this latter computational approach. There the former formula is applied counterfactually to votes observed under the new system. This measures the mechanical allocation difference conditional on the observed post-reform vote distribution.

Rather than recalculating individual elections, Lüscher’s principal empirical analysis estimates how cantonal political outcomes would have developed without the reforms. He finds that Double Pukelsheim substantially reduced vote–seat disproportionality, with stronger improvements in cantons that previously had smaller average district magnitudes (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 129–143). However, Lüscher finds no significant increase in the effective number of parliamentary parties or electoral candidacies. Voter turnout initially declined slightly, but this effect diminished over subsequent elections. These findings distinguish the reform's immediate mechanical consequences from its more limited behavioural effects on parties and voters.(Lüscher, 2024, pp. 143–145) 

The existing literature therefore provides strong evidence that Double Pukelsheim improves proportionality, as well as multiple examples in which smaller parties gain seats. What remains less systematically examined is the magnitude and consistency of the conditional mechanical allocation difference across successive elections. Existing counterfactual studies either focus on only a small number of  individual elections or focus on different aspects like Lüscher. 

This thesis addresses that gap by applying a consistent Hagenbach–Bischoff counterfactual to all 31 available elections in eight transition cantons. Two elections from Graubünden are additionally presented as hypothetical contextual comparisons, since the canton priorly used majority voting. The thesis holds observed post-reform votes constant, applies a common definition of smaller parties, and measures their change in seat share for every election. In contrast to Leuzinger (2018a) and Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher (2011), it does not assume that hypothetical or historical pre-reform alliances would have persisted. The analysis therefore estimates the mechanical allocation difference conditional on the observed votes without introducing an additional behavioral assumption about counterfactual list-alliance formation.


### Expected Effects of the Transition {#sec-expected-effects}

Based on the theoretical considerations outlined in the preceding sections, several effects can be expected from the transition from the Hagenbach–Bischoff method to the Double Pukelsheim system. Under a district-by-district Hagenbach–Bischoff allocation, small district magnitudes create high natural thresholds for winning a parliamentary seat. Votes for parties which fail to win a seat in a district won't contribute elsewhere. This produces ineffective votes and therefore disproportionately disadvantages smaller parties. The biproportional apportionment instead through the upper apportionment pools votes across the whole canton, before it distributes each party's seats among the districts. This should increase the equality of electoral success and reduce vote–seat disproportionality. 
The changed seat-allocation mechanism provides the basis for Hypothesis 1. When holding the observed votes constant, smaller parties are expected to aggregately receive a higher seat-share under Double Pukelsheim than under the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff across the analyzed elections. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2004, pp. 506–508, 513-514 , 518)

Followingly to the prior explanation, the changed seat allocation procedure should have a higher effect in cantons with many low-magnitude districts. This expectation is consistent with Lüscher's finding that the reduction in disproportionality was stronger in cantons with smaller pre-reform average district magnitudes (Lüscher, 2024, pp. 132–133). Furthermore, the effect is expected to depend on the specific institutional design adopted by each canton. Reflecting Switzerland's federal structure, the reformed cantons differ in their use of canton-wide and district-level legal thresholds, majority clauses, and other supplementary adjustments. Explicit electoral thresholds can restrict gains among smaller parties by excluding lists that do not reach the required vote share and may therefore partly offset the greater proportionality of the DP system. (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 18; Lüscher, 2024, pp. 107, 135) In the Zurich 2011 election for example, the SD and Piraten would have received a seat, if there had not been a 5% district-level threshold (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p.1593). The majority clause in constrast has no direct effect on the smaller party seat-share gain, since the cantons ensure in their law, that the seat entitlements according to the upper apportionment must hold. Zug's law for e.g. explicitly states that the majority clause gets deactivated if it is essential to fulfill the upper apportionment seat entitlement. (Kanton Schaffhausen, 1904/2019, Art. 2d para. 1bis and 2(b); Kanton Zug, 2006/2026, § 52e para. 1a, 1b and 2(b); Kanton Graubünden, 2021/2026, Art. 28 para. 2 and 4(b)) 

Valais is a special case, since it pools the votes of 14 subdistricts across 6 electoral districts and not across the whole canton (Lüscher ,2024, p.57). This is expected to limit the proportionality-enhancing effect relative to a canton-wide implementation, especially for parties whose support is dispersed across regions . 

Comparisons across successive elections also provide exploratory context by examining whether smaller parties' mechanical seat-share gains persist or vary over time. No directional trend is hypothesized, as vote distributions, the composition of the smaller-party group, and electoral rules can change between elections.

The estimated difference may additionally depend on the electoral rules used to construct the counterfactual outcomes, including the treatment of list alliances and canton-specific allocation provisions. Together, these expectations provide the foundation for the following hypothesis and exploratory questions concerning differences in smaller parties seat shares.

## Hypotheses

To answer the research question, the thesis tests one main hypothesis concerning how the transition from the Hagenbach–Bischoff system to Double Pukelsheim mechanically affects the seat shares of smaller parties. Complementary exploratory analyses evaluate whether this effect varies with district magnitude, the presence of an explicit electoral threshold, and successive elections since implementation within each canton. Together, these analyses identify both the immediate mechanical and potentially evolving consequences of the electoral-system reform. For all analyses, Graubünden is shown as a contextual comparison and not included in the calculations.

### Hypothesis 1

The Hypothesis 1 researches whether smaller parties when holding votes constant collectively receive a larger seat share under Double Pukelsheim than under the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation. 

For the analysis the following prerequisites and decisions are specified. In each election $e$, smaller parties or electoral lists are those with less than 10% of the vote in the *analyzed area*. The variable *analyzed area* describes the whole canton except in Uri, where the *analyzed area* includes only the four municipalities using the DP-System. The 10% cutoff is chosen with reference to the Swiss Federal Supreme Court's benchmark that natural (implicit) thresholds should not exceed 10% when an electoral system is redesigned (BGE 131 I 74 E. 5.3–5.4; Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 8). This benchmark motivates the definition of smaller parties used in this analysis. As a sensitivity check, the 10% threshold is complemented by an analysis with an 8% and 12% threshold.

Let $S^{DP}_{e}$ and $S^{HB}_{e}$ denote the aggregated number of seats allocated to smaller parties in election $e$ under Double Pukelsheim and the counterfactual Hagenbach–Bischoff system, respectively. Also let $M_e$ denote the total number of seats included in the comparison. Smaller parties' combined gain in seat share, shown for each election in @fig-small-parties-relative, is calculated as follows:

$$
\Delta_e = 100\frac{S^{DP}_{e}-S^{HB}_{e}}{M_e}\quad\text{percentage points}.
$$

The hypothesis uses the unweighted mean, $\bar{\Delta} = \frac{1}{E}\sum_{e=1}^{E}\Delta_e$, so each election counts equally. The analysis also reports a mean weighted by the number of analyzed seats in each election for comparison.

This leads to the following directional hypothesis: 
**$H_1$:** Across the analyzed elections, the mean mechanical difference $\bar{\Delta}$ is positive: electoral lists or list groups with less than 10% of the vote receive, on average, a larger share of the analyzed seats under Double Pukelsheim than under the counterfactual Hagenbach–Bischoff allocation.

As a supplementary and exploratory analysis, it's examined how individual parties' seat-share gains vary across vote-share groups. Here no directional hypothesis regarding the ordering of the groups is formulated. Instead the comparison provides context for the aggregate results by showing which party-sizes experience higher and lower seat-share gains. 

### Exploratory Questions
#### Exploratory question 1: Differences by district magnitude

The first exploratory question investigates the differences by district magnitude. Concretely it asks: Does the gain in smaller parties' seat share under Double Pukelsheim relative to the counterfactual Hagenbach–Bischoff allocation tend to be larger in cantons whose initial district structure was more fragmented? The primary measure is the mean baseline district magnitude. The secondary measure is the relative share of districts with less than 9 seats. Both district measures use a fixed historical baseline from each canton's last pre-reform election, with Schaffhausen adjusted to 60 seats. The secondary measure adds context and can reveal otherwise unobserved patterns for e.g. , the mean may be influenced by a small number of unusually large or small districts. For canton $c$, with $D_{c,0}$ baseline districts and district magnitudes $m_{dc,0}$, the mean district magnitude is

$$
\bar{m}_{c,0}=\frac{1}{D_{c,0}}\sum_{d=1}^{D_{c,0}}m_{dc,0}=\frac{M_{c,0}}{D_{c,0}}.
$$

**A lower baseline mean district magnitude is expected to be associated with a larger average gain for smaller parties.**
 
The secondary measure, is defined followingly:
$c$ denotes the canton and $0$ its pre-reform baseline, $D_{c,0}$ is the number of districts, and $m_{dc,0}$ their seat magnitudes.
$$
q_{c,0}=\frac{1}{D_{c,0}}\sum_{d=1}^{D_{c,0}}\mathbb{1}(m_{dc,0}<9).
$$

The nine-seat cutoff follows the FSC reasoning in Hypothesis 1. Under the natural-quorum approximation $1/(M+1)$, districts with fewer than nine seats impose a threshold above 10%. A larger baseline value of $q_{c,0}$ is therefore expected to be associated with a larger average gain.(BGE 131 I 74 E. 5.3–5.4 ; Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 8) Because of the limited number of transition cantons and their differing rules, this relationship is interpreted descriptively. 

#### Exploratory question 2: Explicit electoral quorums

The second exploratory question, investigates on the differences of the mechanical seat-share gain between elections with and without an explicit electoral threshold. An explicit quorum is a legally specified minimum vote share that a party or list group must reach at a district or cantonal level to qualify for seat allocation. Among the eight cantons of the main analysis, five have applied an explicit quorum. Further details around the details of the implementation of explicit thresholds across the cantons are stated in @sec-adoption. Because such quorums may prevent smaller parties from benefiting from the pooling of votes under Double Pukelsheim, the following directional expectation is formulated:

**On average, the gain of the aggregate smaller parties' seat share under Double Pukelsheim relative to the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation is smaller in elections with an explicit electoral quorum than in elections without one.** 

This comparison is interpreted descriptively because the level and geographical application of the quorums differ across cantons and elections and coincide with other institutional differences.

#### Exploratory question 3: Change across successive elections

How does the gain in smaller parties' seat share under Double Pukelsheim relative to the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation evolve across successive elections within each canton?

This analysis extends Hypothesis 1 by following the seat shares under both allocation rules and their difference $\Delta_e$ from each canton's first election under Double Pukelsheim onward. It assesses whether the overall difference identified in Hypothesis 1 is persistent across elections or driven by particular election-specific outcomes.

Stable positive values of $\Delta_e$ would indicate a persistent mechanical advantage for smaller parties, whereas substantial fluctuations or changes in sign would suggest that the effect is strongly dependent on the circumstances of individual elections. The within-canton perspective further provides a clear separate image for each canton, without mixing their different electoral systems. Given that the smaller parties' seat share, the party composition,  as well as the district magnitudes and electoral rules can change between elections, no directional trend can be hypothesized.

## Research Design and Analysis {#analysis}

### Research Design and Counterfactual Strategy

This thesis uses a deterministic counterfactual reallocation design. The main analysis covers all 31 cantonal parliamentary elections held in the eight transition cantons from Hagenbach-Bischoff to Double Pukelsheim. The two elections from Graubünden are included as contextual comparisons since the canton had previously used a majority voting system. At the computational level, the observations are electoral lists within electoral constituencies and elections, while the primary unit of comparison is the election.

Each election is evaluated under two allocation regimes. The observed outcome is the official allocation under Double Pukelsheim, obtained from the relevant cantonal election authority. The counterfactual outcome is obtained by applying the specified former legal allocation rules to the same election’s observed votes, electoral units, seat magnitudes, and reported list structure. Each election therefore serves as its own comparison. 

The counterfactual is constructed in five steps. 

First, the official election files are imported and standardized to obtain, for every election, electoral unit, and reported list or list group, the observed votes, seat magnitude, and official Double Pukelsheim seats. Party and list labels are harmonized and voter numbers or vote shares are if necessary reconstructed.

Second, the counterfactual inputs are defined by holding the observed votes, electoral units, seat magnitudes, and reported list configuration constant. Joint lists reported as one unit in the official results remain pooled while lists affiliated with the same party, but running independently remain separated.

Third, the specified former allocation regime is applied separately within each electoral unit. All counterfactual allocations use the district-level Hagenbach–Bischoff method described in @sec-hb-method. Where the former cantonal rules contained additional rules such as quorums, majority-clauses, or tie-breaking provisions, these are incorporated into the calculation. The applicable canton-specific rules and features are documented in @sec-assumptions-scope.

Fourth, the counterfactual seats obtained in the individual constituencies are aggregated to the party-election level and merged with the official Double Pukelsheim seat totals.

Finally, the resulting datasets are validated by checking party coverage, vote and seat consistency, electoral-unit seat totals, and the total number of seats allocated under both regimes. Where the source data provide multiple measures of the official Double Pukelsheim result such as upper-apportionment totals, lower apportionment totals, reported list mandates, or elected-candidate counts these measures are additionally reconciled. If exact ties between parties occur, they are if possible resolved with the applicable former cantonal laws. For the two cases in which the tie persisted, both possible seat allocations were presented for the affected parties. This assures, that a seat is never assigned unintentionally through e.g. the arbitrary ordering of rows. The two mentioned unresolved alternatives were observed in Graubünden 2022 and Schwyz 2024 and concerned only parties above the 10% threshold and therefore did not affect the main smaller-party comparison.

With this methodology, the resulting contrast between the observed Double Pukelsheim allocation and the counterfactual is interpreted as a mechanical allocation difference conditional on the observed post-reform votes and not as the reform's complete causal effect. 

### Counterfactual Assumptions and Scope {#sec-assumptions-scope}

Applying the general counterfactual strategy requires several canton-specific decisions concerning electoral rules, list alliances, electoral units, and seat magnitudes. This subsection explains these decisions and defines the scope of the comparison.

Across the nine reform cantons, the counterfactual applies a district-level allocation to the electoral units retained from each observed election. In eight cantons, this generally reconstructs the formerly applicable Hagenbach–Bischoff regime, subject to the exceptions summarized in @tbl-counterfactual-rules. ^[Aargau (Kanton Aargau, 1988/2004, § 12 and § 13(1)(a–b); Staatskanzlei des Kantons Aargau, 2004, section “Neu: 140 statt 200 Mitglieder”); Graubünden (Kanton Graubünden, 2003/2018, Art. 27; hypothetical HB specification based on Kanton Aargau, 1988/2004, § 12 and § 13(1)(a–b)); Nidwalden (BGE 136 I 352, E. 3.2); Schaffhausen (Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 1979, §§ 2, 36–37; Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 2007, pp. 2, 6); Schwyz (Urteil des Bundesgerichts 1C_407/2011 vom 19. März 2012, E. 5.2); Uri (Kanton Uri, 2018, Art. 22–23, “Bisher”; Kanton Uri, 2019, pp. 4, 11); Valais (BGE 140 I 107, Sachverhalt, pp. 108–109; Kanton Wallis, 2004a, Arts. 154–156); Zug (Kanton Zug, 2006, §§ 46–47, 55–56; BGE 136 I 376 E. 4.2, 4.4 and 5.1); and Zurich (Bentz, 2003, p. 2; Kanton Zürich, 1983/2005, §§ 87–88b)] In Graubünden, which previously used Majorz, the Hagenbach–Bischoff allocation is entirely hypothetical and is therefore excluded from the main transition estimate. In every case, the observed votes, electoral-unit seat magnitudes, and reported list structure are held constant. The common Hagenbach–Bischoff procedure is described in @sec-hb-method. This subsection therefore focuses on canton-specific adaptations and limitations of the reconstruction.

Importantly, the comparison in this thesis concerns the complete election-specific allocation regimes previously used in the cantons, rather than only the mathematical difference between the two apportionment algorithms. The observed outcome incorporates the Double-Pukelsheim rules applicable in the respective election, including any explicit electoral quorum. Further the counterfactual applies the relevant former district-level rules to the observed votes and electoral structure. Consequently, differences in seat allocation may reflect both the change in apportionment method and associated differences between the applicable rule packages.


Of all canton-specific provisions in @tbl-counterfactual-rules several do not affect the smaller-party outcomes. For example, the statutory tie-breaking rules in Schaffhausen, Uri, and Zurich were not triggered in any analyzed election. The Schaffhausen rule for calculating the distribution number though, produced differences in two cases: 5,022 rather than 5,023 in Klettgau in 2008 and 2,196 rather than 2,197 in Neuhausen in 2024. These differences changed neither the initial nor the final seat allocation. In Schwyz 2024 and in Graubünden 2022, an unresolved exact tie produced alternative HB allocations for parties above the 10% threshold. Thus it only affected individual party totals but not the aggregated seat total of smaller parties used in the main analysis. The relative-majority allocation in Schaffhausen’s single-seat district was nevertheless applied and remains part of the reconstructed former system. ^[These findings are based on the author’s calculations of the official election data described in Appendix 1. Sources for the applicable legal provisions are provided in the preceding footnote.]

Beyond the statutory allocation rules, the counterfactual requires an assumption about unobserved list alliances. Unlike Leuzinger and Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, this analysis does not carry historical or hypothetical alliances forward. List alliances are in this thesis seen as strategic and election-specific. This means that election-specific, historical alliances cannot simply be assumed to persist across subsequent elections with different parties and vote distributions. Furthermore, the political landscape changed. In Zurich, for example the last Kantonsrat election under Hagenbach–Bischoff took place in 2003. The most recent election in Zurich was held 20 years later in 2023, during that time new parties like the GLP emerged, others like the BDP disappeared and others might have undergone a political shift. (Statistisches Amt des Kantons Zürich 2003, table 3; Amt für Statistik und Daten Kanton Zürich, 2026; Grünliberale Partei Kanton Zürich n.d.). Therefore the counterfactual preserves joint lists or list groups represented as a single unit in the observed election data. But it does not reconstruct historical alliances or assume new alliances between separately reported units. This provides a transparent counterfactual that holds the observed electoral configuration constant and estimates the mechanical allocation difference between the specified election-specific regimes.

The exclusion of unobserved list alliances is an important limitation of the counterfactual. Under Hagenbach–Bischoff, list alliances can pool votes during seat allocation and thereby improve the chances of representation for smaller lists (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1590). If the parties observed under Double Pukelsheim would have formed such alliances under the counterfactual HB regime, excluding them may understate smaller parties' counterfactual HB seat totals and consequently overstate their estimated gain under Double Pukelsheim. However, neither the composition of these hypothetical alliances nor the distribution of any resulting seat gains can be reliably determined. Alliance gains could accrue to larger partners or leave the aggregated representation of parties below the 10% threshold unchanged.

A second research-design choice concerns the electoral units and their seat magnitudes. In most cantons, the reform retained the former territorial districts or municipalities, meaning that the observed electoral units correspond to those used under HB. If regarding the district magnitudes any changes occurred between two periods, then they were applied. The counterfactual therefore holds each observed election’s electoral units and seat magnitudes constant across the two regimes. 

The remaining deviations from this general approach are summarized below.

::: {.callout-note title="Treatment of the Special Cases"}
**Graubünden.** The HB allocation is hypothetical and applied using the common allocation procedure employed elsewhere in the analysis. Its basic formula is taken from the former Aargau law (Kanton Aargau, 1988/2004, § 12 and § 13(1)(a–b)). Thus the observations are shown in grey and excluded from the main transition estimate. In the 2022 election, an unresolved exact tie between the "FDP" and "SP_GRUENE" appears in Rheinwald, to resolve it a hypothetical lot would be needed. The tie, which doesn't affect the aggregated seat total of smaller parties, is therefore retained as an unresolved alternative in the counterfactual.(Kanton Aargau, 1988/2004, § 13; authors calculations using Kanton Graubünden, 2022) Robustness checks using Zurich's party-vote tie-breaker and Schaffhausen's ceiling-based quota preserved all possible allocations across the 39 districts in both 2022 and 2026 (Kanton Zürich, 1983/2005, § 88b; Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 1979, § 36).

**Zug.** Neuheim used Majorz before the reform. An exact Majorz counterfactual cannot be reconstructed because the results of a hypothetical second ballot are unobservable. Neuheim is therefore included using a hypothetical HB allocation.(BGE 136 I 376 E. 5.1; Kanton Zug, 2022a, 2022b, 2022c, 2026) The specific implementation approach adopted for Neuheim has no bearing on the main analysis.

**Uri.** Only Altdorf, Bürglen, Erstfeld, and Schattdorf used Double Pukelsheim in the elections analyzed here. They account for 37 of the Landrat's 64 seats (Standeskanzlei Uri, 2020, p. 1). Uri's vote shares, including the less-than-10% classification of smaller parties, are therefore based only on the four municipalities using Double Pukelsheim, not on the whole canton.

**Valais.** Upper apportionment is conducted separately within six electoral regions rather than canton-wide (Lüscher, 2024, p. 57).

**Schaffhausen.** The parliament was reduced from 80 to 60 seats when Double Pukelsheim was introduced. The counterfactual retains the 60-seat structure. (Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 2007, pp. 1-2, 6).
:::

With the counterfactual rules and scope established, the next subsection describes the official election data and their standardization across cantons.

### Data Sources and Processing {#sec-data-cleaning}

This subsection describes the official election data used in the analysis and explains how the heterogeneous cantonal source files were transformed into a harmonized dataset.

The official election results were obtained primarily from publicly available datasets published by cantonal state chancelleries and statistical offices. Where the data wasn't available online in structured formats, such as CSV or XLSX, they were requested from the responsible cantonal authorities directly. In the case of Schaffhausen no such format was available, therefore the results were extracted from publicly available PDF files. The precise sources and elections covered are reported in Appendix `#ref(<tbl-data-sources>)`{=typst}. The granularity and organization of the source data varied considerably across cantons and elections. In Schwyz, for example, the 2016 results were distributed across 30 municipality-specific csv files, whereas the 2020 and 2024 results were each provided in a single file. In total 110 workbooks or files were used to extract the data.

Party and list names were standardized using readable, clear and consistent abbreviations. The same political organization was assigned a common identifier across cantons and elections, such as "SVP", "GLP", "ALG", and "PIRATEN". The "CVP" and "BDP" remain separately identified before their merger, while "DIEMITTE" is used after the formation of the new party in 2021 (H.-P. Schaub, 2022). In bilingual Valais, French- and German-language labels referring to the same party were harmonized, generally using the German abbreviation for consistency with the other cantons. However, "SP_GAUCHE_CITOYENNE" and "SP_GRUENE_UNABHAENGIGE" were retained as distinct identifiers because they represented separately reported lists with partly different organizations in the background.

The treatment of joint and affiliated lists follows the electoral units reported in the official results. Where several political organizations contested an election on a single joint list, that list was treated as one analytical unit. Examples include "SP_GRUENE" in GR_22 and "FGA_AL_PDA" in ZH_23. It's important to state that joint lists and the list alliances used under Hagenbach-Bischoff differ fundamentally. When forming a joint list, parties run together as a single electoral list (party), while under list alliances the parties run separately and the votes of the alliance parties are pooled later for the seat-allocation. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1590) In addition to joint lists, in some cantons also affiliated or special-interest lists ran as an independent list. This phenomenon occurred especially strongly in Schaffhausen where for example in 2024, seven affiliated lists ran. (Kanton Schaffhausen, n.d.). Since these lists entered the official Double Pukelsheim allocation separately, they were also retained as separate units in the analysis. This decision possibly affects the aggregate seat share of smaller parties.

Beyond the harmonization of party and list names, the cleaning process involved restructuring vote data, identifying the relevant electoral units, and assigning their election-specific seat totals. The source files were converted into comparable tables containing party votes and the seat magnitude of each electoral district. Where results like list totals were repeated, the scripts first checked that these repeated values were consistent and then retained one observation per municipality and list, preventing the totals from being counted multiple times. The geographic preparation depended on the structure of the official files and was widely different across the cantons. In Zurich for e.g municipal party votes were summed within the electoral districts identified by the source variable *Geschaeft* while Aargau’s files already contained district totals which were selected using the *DISTRICT* classification. While in Valais, the 14 sub-districts were assigned to six electoral regions in R according to the official electoral structure, preserving the different geographic levels required for the sub-district-level HB counterfactual and the electoral district-level DP upper apportionment.

District seat magnitudes were obtained from the available official information for each election. They were either already stated in the files, reconstructed with the files' data or if necessary entered manually from official cantonal seat-allocation records .  

The shared finalization function then produced one observation per standardized party or list code and election. It created an election identifier combining the canton abbreviation and election year, such as *ZH_23*, and joined the HB and DP seat totals by party. The final columns were *election_id*, *parties*, *vote_share*, *small_party*, *seats_hb*, *seats_dp*, *parliament_size*, and *seats_allocated_dp*. The last two variables distinguish the full parliament from the seats covered by the comparison, this because of the Canton Uri, where these values are 64 and 37, respectively. District identifiers, raw party votes, and district magnitudes served as intermediate inputs and were not included in the final combined dataset.

Vote shares were derived using the information available in each canton's official election files. For Aargau, Zurich, Zug, and Valais for example, party votes were divided by the corresponding district's seat magnitude to obtain voter equivalents. These quotients were rounded to the nearest integer, with half values rounded upwards, before being summed by party across districts. Each party’s vote share was then calculated as its aggregated voter number divided by the total voter number of all included parties, multiplied by 100.  Uri's published shares refer exclusively to the four relevant municipalites and could therefore be retained. The shared finalization function rounded all vote shares to four decimal places.

The Double Pukelsheim results were assembled separately within the canton-specific scripts from official seat tables, municipal allocations, or elected-candidate records. Each script supplied its election-specific DP results to the shared finalization function, which joined them to the HB counterfactuals by standardized party identifier. Validation routines checked electoral-unit coverage and seat totals and where alternative representations were available, reconciled candidate counts or aggregated lower allocations with reported list mandates or upper-apportionment totals. District-level consistency checks and final allocation totals were applied according to the available source structure. Uri’s allocation checks covered the 37 proportional seats included in the analysis. Unresolved Hagenbach-Bischoff ties were retained as alternative allocations.

One of the consistency checks revealed an error in the Zurich 2011 election data. There the party-votes total for the "SP" was doubled across all constituencies. The mistake was found through the comparison of the summed party votes with the reported unit totals and cross-checking candidate and supplementary votes. Followingly, the error was reported to the Statistical Office of the Canton of Zurich. They confirmed the mistake and resolved the underlying cause, which was that a duplicate "SP" entry in the list-to-party mapping table had caused double counting during the aggregation of the official municipal results. The corrected dataset was uploaded and is used in this analysis. (S.Graf, personal communication, 2026-09-11)

All processing was implemented in the canton-specific R scripts in *data_cleaning_cantons*, supported by the shared functions in *00_functions.R*. Each *process_canton_*()* function combined its cleaned elections into a cantonal dataset. These nine datasets were subsequently appended row-wise using *bind_rows()* to create *all_elections*, preserving one observation per standardized party or list and election. Detailed election data sources and legal bases are documented in Appendix 1, with the cleaning code provided on the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/MB20030/BA_Thesis) and on the HSG Thesis Management Platform.

```{r data-setup}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(out.width = "100%")

}

# Load the allocation functions and canton-specific cleaning scripts.
```

### Measures and Analytical Strategy {#sec-measures}

The *analyzed_area* comprises the whole canton except in Uri, where it covers only Altdorf, Bürglen, Erstfeld, and Schattdorf, the four municipalities using Double Pukelsheim. The variable *seats_allocated_dp* records the number of seats covered by the comparison, while *parliament_size* records the full size of the cantonal parliament. These values are equal in all analyzed cantons except Uri.

For the purposes of this thesis, a smaller party is defined as an electoral list or list group with a vote share below 10% in the analyzed area. Youth lists and other affiliated lists are treated as separate analytical units whenever they enter the official Double Pukelsheim allocation separately. Accordingly, the term *party* refers to the standardized electoral list or list group recorded in the dataset and does not necessarily correspond to a broader organizational party family. *Smaller parties* are identified separately for each election using their observed vote shares. The same set of smaller parties is then used when comparing the two seat allocations within that election.

The main analysis compares the combined seat shares of smaller parties within each election. For this purpose, the seats of all lists below the 10% vote-share threshold are summed separately under Double Pukelsheim and Hagenbach–Bischoff. Each total is divided by the number of analyzed seats, recorded in *seats_allocated_dp*, and multiplied by 100 to obtain the corresponding seat share as a percentage. This produces one aggregate seat-share difference per election. Using *seats_allocated_dp* ensures that the results for Uri are not distorted.

The election-level outcome is the difference between these two seat shares, denoted by $\Delta_e$ and defined in Hypothesis 1. Positive values indicate that smaller parties collectively receive a larger seat share under Double Pukelsheim while negative values indicate a smaller share. A negative or positive aggregate difference, does not mean that each included party loses or gains seats respectively. 

Hypothesis 1 is assessed using the average seat-share difference aross all 31 elections. In that analysis every election receives equal weight, which means that cantons with more elections held under DP are influencing the average more strongly. Since the parliament sizes differ, a supplementary weighted mean is added, where more weight to bigger parliaments is given. To better display the variation and typical gain, the median ,the first and third quartiles are reported additionally. The main summaries show Graubünden only contextually for the reasons set out in @sec-assumptions-scope.

All three exploratory analyses are descriptive. They examine differences across institutional settings and successive elections without isolating the causal effects of individual electoral rules.

For EQ1, election-level seat-share gains are first averaged within each canton. These canton-level outcomes are examined against mean district magnitude and the share of districts below nine seats. These two measures are calculated from the same fixed allocation in each cantons last pre-reform election and with the Schaffhausen parliament adjusted to 60 seats. These historical characteristics are held fixed when comparing the canton-level average gains across the analyzed elections. Uri covers the same four municipalities included in the HB–DP comparison, and Valais's district count refers to its 14 Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation districts. Both district measures are calculated once per canton from this baseline and are held fixed across its analyzed elections. For each measure, cantons are grouped below or at or above its unweighted mean across the eight transition cantons. Group means give each canton equal weight, and the group difference is calculated as below-mean minus at-or-above-mean. Graubünden is shown only for context. The historical reference year applies to all district measures. Historical seat allocations are documented in the cantonal publications and court judgments cited below.^[Sources by canton and reference year: Aargau 2005 (Kanton Aargau, 2004); Graubünden 2018 (Kanton Graubünden, n.d.); Nidwalden 2010 (BGE 136 I 352, E. 3.5); Schaffhausen 2004, adjusted to 60 seats (Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 2007, Table 1, p. 2); Schwyz 2012 (Urteil des Bundesgerichts 1C_407/2011 vom 19. März 2012, Sachverhalt A); Uri 2016 (Standeskanzlei Uri, 2016, p. 5); Valais 2013 (BGE 140 I 107, Sachverhalt A); Zug 2010 (Staatskanzlei des Kantons Zug, 2010, p. 92); Zurich 2003 (Regierungsrat des Kantons Zürich, 2002).] Later district magnitudes may change, so the district measures describe associations with the initial structure. For Schaffhausen, the 2004 structure is adjusted from 80 to 60 seats using the published hypothetical allocation in the government's reform report (Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 2007, Table 1, p. 2). The election-specific Hagenbach-Bischoff to Double Pukelsheim allocations are unchanged.

For EQ2, elections are grouped by whether or not an explicit electoral quorum applied under Double Pukelsheim. Within each group, the mean of $\Delta_e$ gives each election equal weight, so cantons with more observed elections contribute more. The group difference is calculated as the mean without a quorum minus the mean with one. Graubünden is shown for context and excluded from both means. Since the observations differ structurally in terms of quorum levels, geographical scope and others, the analysis is only descriptive.

To examine successive elections, the seat-share difference $\Delta_e$ is plotted separately for each canton and its successive elections. The aim is to analyze whether the mechanical seat-share gain persists across elections. To identify possible influencing factors, they are noted next to the election in which they occurred. Later changes and fluctuations are interpreted with the help of the additional context provided by the notes. Besides the separate analyis of each canton, the results are also set into the between-canton context to possibly identify general patterns.
