#### Hypothesis 1: Smaller parties' seat-share difference {#sec-h1-results}

@fig-small-parties-relative compares the aggregate smaller parties' combined seat shares under the observed Double Pukelsheim allocation and the counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation for every available election. Smaller parties are defined as parties with less than 10% of the vote share in the analyzed area. This seat-share difference allows comparisons across elections with different numbers of analyzed seats. 

```{r}
#| label: h1-data-and-plot-setup
#| include: false
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Restrict the tie check to parties below the 10% vote-share threshold.
small_party_rows <- all_elections |>
  filter(small_party == 1L)

# A slash marks alternative HB seat totals from an unresolved draw.
if (any(str_detect(small_party_rows$seats_hb, fixed("/")))) {
  stop("Resolve smaller-party HB ties before plotting.")
}

# Aggregate smaller parties within each election under both seat rules.
small_party_summary <- all_elections |>
  group_by(election_id) |>
  summarise(
    parliament_size = first(parliament_size),
    seats_allocated_dp = first(seats_allocated_dp),
    vote_share_small_parties = sum(vote_share[small_party == 1L]),
    # Only smaller-party seats enter the HB–DP comparison.
    seats_hb = sum(as.integer(seats_hb[small_party == 1L])),
    seats_dp = sum(seats_dp[small_party == 1L]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    is_graubuenden = str_starts(election_id, "GR_"),
    # Express the DP gain as a share of seats included in the comparison.
    seat_gain_pp = 100 * (seats_dp - seats_hb) / seats_allocated_dp
  )

# Put both systems on separate rows for plotting and calculate seat shares.
small_party_plot_data <- small_party_summary |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(seats_hb, seats_dp),
    names_to = "system",
    values_to = "seats_small_parties"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    seat_share_small_parties = 100 * seats_small_parties / seats_allocated_dp,
    # Fix the legend order across both figures.
    system = factor(recode(system, seats_hb = "Hagenbach-Bischoff", seats_dp = "Double Pukelsheim"),
                    levels = c("Hagenbach-Bischoff", "Double Pukelsheim"))
  )

# Summarize election-level gains and the mean weighted by analyzed seats.
h1_stats <- small_party_summary |>
  filter(!is_graubuenden) |>
  summarise(
    elections = n(), mean_gain = mean(seat_gain_pp),
    weighted_mean_gain = weighted.mean(seat_gain_pp, seats_allocated_dp),
    q1 = quantile(seat_gain_pp, .25), median = median(seat_gain_pp),
    q3 = quantile(seat_gain_pp, .75),
    above_five = sum(seat_gain_pp > 5)
  )

small_party_plot <- function(x, x_title, label, percent = FALSE) {
  # Label selected examples
  labelled_elections <- c("UR_20", "SZ_24", "SH_16", "ZH_15", "VS_21", "ZH_11")
  gain_labelled_elections <- labelled_elections # add gain to the label
  # Keep all endpoints in one repel layer
  label_data <- small_party_plot_data |>
    mutate(
      plot_label = if_else(
        system == "Double Pukelsheim" &
          (election_id %in% labelled_elections | is_graubuenden),
        .data[[label]], ""
      ),
      plot_label = if_else(
        plot_label != "" & election_id %in% gain_labelled_elections,
        sprintf("%s (%+.1f pp)", plot_label, seat_gain_pp),
        plot_label
      ),
      label_colour = if_else(is_graubuenden, "Context only", as.character(system))
    )
  # Repulsion needs obstacles along horizontal comparison lines
  line_obstacles <- small_party_plot_data |>
    group_by(election_id) |>
    reframe(
      !!x := seq(min(.data[[x]]), max(.data[[x]]), length.out = 25),
      vote_share_small_parties = first(vote_share_small_parties),
      plot_label = "", label_colour = "Context only"
    )
  ggplot(small_party_plot_data, aes(x = .data[[x]], y = vote_share_small_parties,
                                   color = system, shape = system)) +
  geom_abline(
      intercept = 0,
      slope = 1,
      linetype = "dashed",
      colour = "grey60",
      linewidth = 0.4,
      show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    # Connect the two outcomes from each election
    geom_line(aes(group = election_id), color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_point(data = filter(small_party_plot_data, !is_graubuenden), size = 3.2) +
    geom_point(data = filter(small_party_plot_data, is_graubuenden),
           color = "grey60", size = 3.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
    # Repel selected text labels from all endpoints and comparison lines.
    geom_text_repel(
      data = bind_rows(label_data, line_obstacles), inherit.aes = FALSE,
      aes(x = .data[[x]], y = vote_share_small_parties,
          label = plot_label, color = label_colour),
      size = 3.2, show.legend = FALSE, max.overlaps = Inf,
      box.padding = 0.4, point.padding = 0.15, force = 3,
      max.time = Inf, max.iter = 30000,
      min.segment.length = 0, segment.color = "grey65",
      segment.size = 0.35, seed = 2026
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("Hagenbach-Bischoff" = "#D55E00",
                                  "Double Pukelsheim" = "#0072B2",
                                  "Context only" = "grey60"),
                       breaks = c("Hagenbach-Bischoff", "Double Pukelsheim")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c("Hagenbach-Bischoff" = 16,
                                  "Double Pukelsheim" = 17)) +
    # Format the x-axis as percentages only in the relative figure.
    scale_x_continuous(labels = if (percent) \(x) paste0(x, "%") else waiver(),
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.12))) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.12))) +
    labs(title = "Representation of Smaller Parties Across Elections",
         subtitle = "Observed Double Pukelsheim and counterfactual Hagenbach-Bischoff allocations",
         caption = wrap_plot_caption(
           "Grey lines connect the two allocations for the same election.",
           "The dashed diagonal marks equality between aggregate vote and seat shares.",
           "Points above it indicate underrepresentation; points below it indicate overrepresentation.",
           width = 116
         ),
         x = x_title, y = "Aggregated vote share of smaller parties (%)",
         color = "Electoral system", shape = "Electoral system") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_text(size = 11),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11), axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
          plot.caption.position = "plot",
          plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 11, lineheight = 1.1,
                                      margin = margin(t = 8)),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}
# Adding sensitivity check with 8% smaller-parties threshold
sensitivity_8 <- all_elections |> 
  filter(!str_starts(election_id, "GR_")) |>
  group_by(election_id) |>
  summarise(
    small_parties = sum(vote_share < 8),
    gain_pp = 100 * (
      sum(seats_dp[vote_share < 8]) -
      sum(as.integer(seats_hb[vote_share < 8]))
    ) / first(seats_allocated_dp)
  )
# second sensitivity check with 12% threshold
sensitivity_12 <- all_elections |> 
  filter(!str_starts(election_id, "GR_")) |>
  group_by(election_id) |>
  summarise(
    small_parties = sum(vote_share < 12),
    gain_pp = 100 * (
      sum(seats_dp[vote_share < 12]) -
      sum(as.integer(seats_hb[vote_share < 12]))
    ) / first(seats_allocated_dp)
  )

mean(sensitivity_8$gain_pp)
mean(sensitivity_12$gain_pp)

# Elections with parties below 8% but no aggregate seat gain under DP
no_gain_8 <- sensitivity_8 |>
  filter(small_parties > 0, gain_pp <= 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-small-parties-relative
#| fig-cap: "Smaller party seat-shares under HB and DP" 
#| fig-width: 8.3
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Reuse the plot with seat shares and one election identifier per comparison.
small_party_plot("seat_share_small_parties", "Aggregated seat share of smaller parties (%)", "election_id", TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Hypothesis 1 summary"}
Across all `r h1_stats$elections` transition elections (Graubünden excluded), the unweighted mean gain in smaller parties' share of analyzed seats was `r sprintf("%.1f", h1_stats$mean_gain)` percentage points (Q1: `r sprintf("%.1f", h1_stats$q1)`; median: `r sprintf("%.1f", h1_stats$median)`; Q3: `r sprintf("%.1f", h1_stats$q3)`). The mean weighted by each election's number of analyzed seats was `r sprintf("%.1f", h1_stats$weighted_mean_gain)` percentage points. `r h1_stats$above_five` individual elections exceeded five percentage points.
:::

These results descriptively support Hypothesis 1 and indicate that smaller parties indeed in the 31 elections held, receive a larger share of the analyzed seats under Double Pukelsheim than under Hagenbach-Bischoff. This effect is partically evident, through that in every election where small parties contested (every election but Uri 2020), they aggregately received a larger seat share. This finding is in accordance with Leuzinger's observation that smaller parties tend to profit from the transition (Leuzinger, 2018a, p.42). The weighted mean, unweighted mean and median are all relatively close to each other, indicating that the effect is not driven by a few elections with many seats and that the positive effect isn't determined by extreme outliers. 

The average gain differs across the cantons. For example the Canton of Schaffhausen has a stable high seat gain for smaller parties. There the high seat-share gain may be partially explained through the decision to treat affiliated parties as independent lists. Therefore these affiliated lists were classified as smaller parties, if they didn't reach the 10% threshold themselves and with that increase the relative gain for smaller parties. When the affiliated parties were attributed to their mother parties, the gain dropped from 15.67 to 8.67 percentage points. No matter the treatment of the affiliated lists, are the gains in Schaffhausen comparatively high. By contrast, the gains were constantly relatively low in Uri and Schwyz, where on average 0.5 and 1.66 smaller parties contested per election. 

The general finding is further robust to alternative definitions of smaller parties. Using a vote-share cutoff of less than 8%, the mean gain is `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(sensitivity_8$gain_pp))` percentage points. The smaller parties also collectively receive a higher seat share under Double Pukelsheim in `r sum(sensitivity_8$gain_pp > 0)` of the `r sum(sensitivity_8$small_parties > 0)` elections where at least one party with a vote-share below 8% contested. The exception is  `r paste(str_replace(no_gain_8$election_id, "_", " 20"), collapse = " and ")` , where the aggregated difference is zero and the upper-allocation process was not done across the whole canton. With a cutoff of less than 12%, the mean gain is `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(sensitivity_12$gain_pp))` percentage points. Regarding the collectively higher seat share in this case, in  `r sum(sensitivity_12$gain_pp > 0)` of the `r sum(sensitivity_12$small_parties > 0)` relevant elections, the smaller parties received a higher seat-share gain. The Uri 2020, is again the exception, where no party with less than 12% vote-share ran.

As a further sensitivity and robustness check, the results were tested with a leave one canton out check. In that check the means are recalculated with each canton being omitted once. The positive seat-share gain persisted across each check. This persistance, fits the finding that in 30 of 31 elections, a positive aggregated seat-share gain for smaller parties was observed. The detailed results for the checks can be found in the Appendix in @sec-leave-one-out. 

The prior measures deliver a profound picture over the aggregated seat-share gain of smaller parties, but they don't reveal whether smaller parties profited independently, and which category of smaller parties profits most from the transition. This is analyzed in the following subanalysis. 
```{r}
#| label: fig-party-size-gains
#| fig-cap: "Mechanical seat-share gains by party vote-share group"
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| echo: false
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)

party_size_plot_data <- all_elections |>
  filter(
    vote_share >= 0,
    vote_share < 15 # Filter only parties with vote-shares below 15%
  ) |>
  mutate(
    comparison = if_else(str_starts(election_id, "GR_"),
                         "Graubünden (context)", "Transition cantons"),
    gain_pp = 100 * ( # Gain as percentage points of analyzed seats.
      seats_dp - as.integer(seats_hb)
    ) / seats_allocated_dp,

    size_group = cut( # Group parties by their election-specific vote share.
      vote_share,
      breaks = c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15), # Eight boundaries define seven groups.
      labels = c(
        "0-<2%", "2-<4%", "4-<6%",
        "6-<8%", "8-<10%", "10-<12%", "12-<15%"
      ),
      right = FALSE # Include lower boundaries: 4% enters 4-<6%.
    )
  )

# Keep the transition sample separate for all summaries and counts.
party_size_data <- party_size_plot_data |>
  filter(comparison == "Transition cantons")

party_size_means <- party_size_data |>
  group_by(size_group) |>
  summarise(mean_gain_pp = mean(gain_pp), n = n(), .groups = "drop") # Equal weight per party-election.

ggplot(party_size_data, aes(x = size_group, y = gain_pp)) +
  # Shade the groups outside the smaller-party definition
  annotate(
    "rect", xmin = 5.5, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#F2F2F2"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
  xintercept = 5.5,
  linetype = "dashed",
  colour = "grey50",
  linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    colour = "grey50",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = party_size_plot_data,
    aes(colour = comparison, shape = comparison),
    position = position_jitter(
      width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 2026 # Separate dots horizontally only.
    ),
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = party_size_means,
    aes(y = mean_gain_pp), # Mark each group's mean.
    colour = "#000000",
    shape = 18,
    size = 4
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = party_size_means,
    aes(y = mean_gain_pp, label = sprintf("%.2f", mean_gain_pp)), # Label means in pp.
    nudge_x = 0.18,
    hjust = 0,
    colour = "#000000",
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    labels = setNames(
      paste0(
        party_size_means$size_group,
        "\n(n = ", party_size_means$n, ")"
      ),
      party_size_means$size_group
    )
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("Transition cantons" = "#0072B2", "Graubünden (context)" = "#707070"),
    breaks = c("Transition cantons", "Graubünden (context)"), name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c("Transition cantons" = 16, "Graubünden (context)" = 1),
    breaks = c("Transition cantons", "Graubünden (context)"), name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Party vote-share group in the analyzed area",
    y = "Seat-share gain under DP relative to HB (pp)",
    caption = wrap_plot_caption(
      "Black diamonds and labels: transition-canton group means (pp).",
      "n counts transition observations only.\n",
      "Grey shading: vote-share groups outside the smaller-party definition.\n",
      "Grey open circles: Graubünden for context",
      width = 100
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 11, lineheight = 1.1,
                                margin = margin(t = 8))
  )


```

The analysis shows, that the vast majority of the smaller parties below 10% not only profit aggregately from the transition but also independently. The summary of the `r nrow(party_size_data)` party-election observations shows that parties between 4-6% vote share tend to profit the most from the implementation of the Double Pukelsheim. For parties with more than 10% the seat-share gain is on average markedly lower and reaches for parties above 12 and below 15% a point, where the parties with 0.46 percentage points barely profit anymore from the implementation. Also parties on the other side of the scale with less than 2% only benefit slightly, there 45 of 66 observed parties receive no seats under either allocation. Overall, the analysis shows that smaller parties tend to profit from the implementation whereas bigger parties on average subsequently lose their prior advantage under the old system. To be able to identify a possible gradual pattern, the analysis was also done without grouping. The figure there shows no clear monotonic relationship. Furthermore, substantial variation between parties of the same vote share be seen throughout the analysis. Another observation is, that parties with a very low share cluster around zero, while positive gains occur across most of the remaining range. Furthermore, most negative observations appear in the upper end of the range. The figure can be found in the Appendix in @sec-additional-analysis.

To sum up the analysis of Hypothesis 1: It covers all 31 cantonal parliamentary elections held under Double Pukelsheim in Switzerland from the cantons that transitioned from Hagenbach-Bischoff. Across these elections, smaller parties received under all definitions of smaller parties, a higher aggregate seat share under Double Pukelsheim. This pattern also persisted throughout almost every within election comparison of smaller parties. Furthermore, the analysis showed that most smaller parties also profit on an individual basis from the transition. These findings are based on the mechanical allocation difference conditional on the observed votes and specified counterfactual rules and therefore do not capture the whole transition effect. The next section examines whether the magnitude of this effect is associated with 'the cantons' district magnitudes. 

#### Exploratory question 1: Differences by district magnitude

This section examines historical district structure using mean district magnitude and the share of districts with fewer than nine seats. @tbl-district-magnitude reports these measures alongside district counts and reference years. Both measures refer to the fixed historical baseline defined in @sec-measures, with Schaffhausen adjusted to 60 seats. Graubünden is shown for context only.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-district-magnitude
#| tbl-cap: "Pre-reform district structure by canton"
#| tbl-colwidths: [15, 15, 20, 20, 30]
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

eq1_env <- new.env(parent = globalenv()) 

sys.source(here("data_cleaning_cantons", "00_functions.R"), eq1_env) # Load the shared cleaning functions 
eq1_env$district_registry <- list() # create empty list to store the values
eq1_env$original_finalize <- eq1_env$finalize_election_data # Keep the original function before wrapping it.
eq1_env$finalize_election_data <- function(
    hb_results, dp_results, canton, year, parliament_size = NULL) {
  caller <- parent.frame() # Access the reader that called this function and its local district table.
  table_name <- switch(canton, AG = "districts", GR = "hb_by_district",
                       SH = "district_totals", ZH = "district_seats",
                       "district_results") 
  district_name <- if (canton == "AG") "location_name" else "district" # Standardize Aargau's name column.
  districts <- get(table_name, envir = caller, inherits = FALSE) |> 
    transmute(district = .data[[district_name]], district_seats) |> # Keep only district names and seat counts
    distinct() # Remove repeated identical rows.
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(districts$district), !anyNA(districts),
            all(districts$district_seats > 0),
            all(districts$district_seats == floor(districts$district_seats))) # Stop if names or seat counts are invalid.
  result <- original_finalize(hb_results, dp_results, canton, year, parliament_size) # Calculate the usual election output
  stopifnot(sum(districts$district_seats) == first(result$seats_allocated_dp)) # District seats must match DP seat coverage.
  id <- first(result$election_id) # Election identifier
  district_registry[[id]] <<- districts |>
    mutate(election_id = id, canton = canton, year = year, .before = 1) 
  result # Return the original election output 
}
environment(eq1_env$finalize_election_data) <- eq1_env 

eq1_codes <- c("AG", "GR", "NW", "SH", "SZ", "UR", "VS", "ZG", "ZH") # Cantons included, with GR for context.
for (code in eq1_codes) { # Load each canton's reader into the separate workspace.
  expressions <- parse(here("data_cleaning_cantons", paste0("canton_", code, ".R")),
                       encoding = "UTF-8") 
  for (expression in expressions) {
    
    if (is.call(expression) && identical(expression[[1]], as.name("print"))) next
    eval(expression, envir = eq1_env) # Run the remaining definitions in the separate workspace.
  }
}
eq1_parties <- map_dfr(eq1_codes, function(code) {
  get(paste0("process_canton_", code), envir = eq1_env)() # Run each reader; map_dfr stacks the resulting rows.
})
eq1_districts <- bind_rows(eq1_env$district_registry) # Stack the captured district tables across elections.
stopifnot(n_distinct(eq1_parties$election_id) == 33L,
          n_distinct(eq1_districts$election_id) == 33L,
          isTRUE(all.equal(arrange(eq1_parties, election_id, parties),
                           arrange(all_elections, election_id, parties)))) 

# Use the same election-level outcome as H1; validate analyzed seat coverage.
eq1_elections <- eq1_districts |>
  group_by(canton, election_id, year) |> # Calculate coverage separately for each election.
  summarise(
    districts = n(), analyzed_seats = sum(district_seats), # Count districts and total their seats.
    .groups = "drop" # Return an ordinary, ungrouped table.
  ) |>
  left_join(small_party_summary |>
              select(election_id, seats_allocated_dp, seat_gain_pp),
            by = "election_id") # Match each election to H1's smaller-party gain
stopifnot(!anyNA(eq1_elections),
          all(eq1_elections$analyzed_seats == eq1_elections$seats_allocated_dp)) # Check complete matches and equal seat coverage.

# Fixed last-pre-reform allocations. Named vectors preserve district provenance.

eq1_baseline_seats <- list( 
  AG = c(Aarau = 16, Baden = 30, Bremgarten = 16, Brugg = 11, Kulm = 9,
         Laufenburg = 6, Lenzburg = 12, Muri = 7, Rheinfelden = 10,
         Zofingen = 15, Zurzach = 8),
  GR = c(Alvaschein = 2, Avers = 1, Belfort = 1, Berguen = 1, Bregaglia = 1,
         Brusio = 1, Calanca = 1, Chur = 20, Churwalden = 1, Davos = 6,
         Disentis = 4, Domleschg = 3, Fuenf_Doerfer = 12, Ilanz = 6,
         Jenaz = 1, Klosters = 3, Kueblis = 1, Lumnezia_Lugnez = 2,
         Luzein = 1, Maienfeld = 4, Mesocco = 2, Oberengadin = 8,
         Poschiavo = 2, Ramosch = 1, Rhaezuens = 7, Rheinwald = 1,
         Roveredo = 3, Ruis = 1, Safien = 1, Schams = 1, Schanfigg = 2,
         Schiers = 3, Seewis = 1, Suot_Tasna = 3, Sur_Tasna = 1,
         Surses = 1, Thusis = 4, Trins = 5, Val_Muestair = 1),
  NW = c(Stans = 11, Ennetmoos = 3, Dallenwil = 3, Stansstad = 6,
         Oberdorf = 5, Buochs = 8, Ennetbuergen = 6, Wolfenschiessen = 3,
         Beckenried = 5, Hergiswil = 8, Emmetten = 2),
  # Published adjustment of the 2004 district structure to a 60-seat parliament.
  SH = c(Schaffhausen = 28, Neuhausen = 8, Klettgau = 12, Reiat = 7,
         Stein = 4, Buchberg_Ruedlingen = 1),
  SZ = c(Schwyz = 10, Arth = 7, Ingenbohl = 6, Muothathal = 2, Steinen = 2,
         Sattel = 1, Rothenthurm = 1, Oberiberg = 1, Unteriberg = 1,
         Lauerz = 1, Steinerberg = 1, Morschach = 1, Alpthal = 1, Illgau = 1,
         Riemenstalden = 1, Gersau = 1, Lachen = 5, Altendorf = 4,
         Galgenen = 3, Vorderthal = 1, Innerthal = 1, Schuebelbach = 6,
         Tuggen = 2, Wangen = 3, Reichenburg = 2, Einsiedeln = 10,
         Kuessnacht = 8, Wollerau = 4, Freienbach = 10, Feusisberg = 3),
  UR = c(Altdorf = 15, Buerglen = 7, Erstfeld = 6, Schattdorf = 9), 
  VS = c(Goms = 2, Oestlich_Raron = 2, Brig = 12, Visp = 12,
         Westlich_Raron = 4, Leuk = 6, Siders = 17, Ering = 5, Sitten = 17,
         Gundis = 10, Martinach = 16, Entremont = 6, St_Maurice = 5,
         Monthey = 16),
  ZG = c(Zug = 19, Oberaegeri = 4, Unteraegeri = 6, Menzingen = 3,
         Baar = 15, Cham = 10, Huenenberg = 6, Steinhausen = 6, Risch = 6,
         Walchwil = 3, Neuheim = 2),
  ZH = c(Zuerich_1_2 = 5, Zuerich_3_9 = 13, Zuerich_4_5 = 5,
         Zuerich_6_10 = 9, Zuerich_7_8 = 7, Zuerich_11_12 = 11,
         Dietikon = 11, Affoltern = 6, Horgen = 16, Meilen = 13, Hinwil = 11,
         Uster = 16, Pfaeffikon = 7, Winterthur_Stadt = 13,
         Winterthur_Land = 7, Andelfingen = 4, Buelach = 16, Dielsdorf = 10)
)
eq1_baseline_years <- c(AG = 2005L, GR = 2018L, NW = 2010L, SH = 2004L,
                        SZ = 2012L, UR = 2016L, VS = 2013L, ZG = 2010L,
                        ZH = 2003L) # Historical reference years
eq1_baseline_totals <- c(AG = 140, GR = 120, NW = 60, SH = 60, SZ = 100,
                         UR = 37, VS = 130, ZG = 80, ZH = 180) # Expected seat totals
stopifnot(identical(names(eq1_baseline_seats), eq1_codes),
          all(map_lgl(eq1_baseline_seats, function(x) {
            !anyNA(x) && !anyDuplicated(names(x)) &&
              all(x > 0 & x == floor(x))
          })),
          all(map_dbl(eq1_baseline_seats, sum) == eq1_baseline_totals)) # Check canton order, valid district entries, and seat totals.
eq1_baseline <- imap_dfr(eq1_baseline_seats, function(seats, code) {
  tibble(
    canton = code,
    reference_year = eq1_baseline_years[[code]],
    baseline_districts = length(seats),
    mean_magnitude_baseline = mean(seats),
    share_below9_pct_baseline = 100 * mean(seats < 9)
  )
})

eq1_cantons <- eq1_elections |>
  group_by(canton) |> # Collapse election-level outcomes into one row per canton.
  summarise(
    elections = n(), districts_min = min(districts), districts_max = max(districts),
    mean_gain_pp = mean(seat_gain_pp), .groups = "drop" # Average outcomes across elections, giving each election equal weight.
  ) |>
  left_join(eq1_baseline, by = "canton") # Attach fixed historical predictors
stopifnot(!anyNA(eq1_cantons),
          all(eq1_cantons$districts_min == eq1_cantons$districts_max),
          all(eq1_cantons$baseline_districts == eq1_cantons$districts_min)) # Check no missing values and consistent district counts.

# The cutoff for each measure is the unweighted mean across transition cantons.
eq1_points <- eq1_cantons |>
  select(canton, mean_gain_pp, ends_with("_baseline")) |> # Keep the outcome and two baseline measures for plotting.
  pivot_longer(-c(canton, mean_gain_pp), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |> # One row per canton and measure.
  group_by(metric) |> # Each measure has its own cutoff and groups.
  mutate(cutoff = mean(value[canton != "GR"]), # Unweighted mean of the eight transition cantons; exclude GR.
         group = case_when(canton == "GR" ~ "GR: context only",
                           value < cutoff ~ "Below mean",
                           TRUE ~ "At/above mean")) |> # GR gets a context label; equality with the cutoff goes in the upper group.
  ungroup() |> # Remove grouping before setting display labels.
  mutate(metric = factor(
    metric,
    levels = c("mean_magnitude_baseline", "share_below9_pct_baseline"),
    labels = c("Mean district size (seats)", "Districts below 9 seats (%)")),
    group = factor(group, c("Below mean", "At/above mean", "GR: context only"))) # Factors control panel and legend order.
eq1_groups <- eq1_points |>
  filter(canton != "GR") |> # Context canton does not contribute to group comparisons.
  group_by(metric, group) |> # Summarize each below-mean or upper group separately for each measure.
  summarise(cantons = n(), mean_gain_pp = mean(mean_gain_pp),
            members = paste(sort(canton), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") # Count cantons, average their gains equally, and list members.
eq1_differences <- eq1_groups |>
  select(metric, group, mean_gain_pp) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = mean_gain_pp) |> # Put the two group means in separate columns.
  mutate(below_minus_above_pp = `Below mean` - `At/above mean`) # Negative = the below-mean group gained less.
eq1_cutoffs <- eq1_points |>
  distinct(metric, cutoff) # One cutoff per measure, used in the text and dashed lines.

knitr::kable( # Render table
  eq1_cantons |>
    transmute(
      Canton = canton, Districts = baseline_districts,
      `Reference year` = reference_year,
      `Mean seats` = sprintf("%.2f", mean_magnitude_baseline), # Display two decimals; underlying values remain unrounded.
      `Below 9 seats (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", share_below9_pct_baseline) # Display this percentage with one decimal.
    ),
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r") # Left-align canton names; right-align the numerical columns.
)
```
*Notes*  To compute the measures for Uri, only the four DP constitutiencies (municipalities) were taken.

@fig-district-magnitude relates each district measure to the canton-level mean gain in smaller parties' seat share. The cutoffs are defined by the mean of the eight relevant cantons and are the following: `r sprintf("%.2f", eq1_cutoffs$cutoff[eq1_cutoffs$metric == "Mean district size (seats)"])` seats for the unweighted mean magnitude and `r sprintf("%.2f", eq1_cutoffs$cutoff[eq1_cutoffs$metric == "Districts below 9 seats (%)"])`% for the share below nine seats. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-district-magnitude
#| fig-cap: "Smaller-party seat-share gains by historical district structure"
#| fig-width: 8.3
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

eq1_colours <- c("Below mean" = "#0072B2", "At/above mean" = "#D55E00",
                 "GR: context only" = "#8A8A8A") 
eq1_scatter <- ggplot(eq1_points, aes(value, mean_gain_pp, colour = group)) + # x = district measure; y = canton gain
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70", linewidth = .35) + # Reference line where DP and HB give equal smaller-party shares.
  geom_vline(data = eq1_cutoffs, aes(xintercept = cutoff), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60", linewidth = .4) + 
  geom_point(size = 2.8) + # One point per canton in each panel.
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = canton), seed = 1, size = 3.3,
                  max.overlaps = Inf, show.legend = FALSE) + # Repel canton labels
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) + # Two panels in two columns, separate x scales because units differ.
  scale_colour_manual(values = eq1_colours, drop = FALSE) + 
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(.12, .15))) + # Add space at the plot edges for labels.
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(.12, .15))) +
  labs(x = "District measure (fixed historical baseline)",
       y = "Mean smaller-party seat-share gain (pp)", colour = NULL, 
       caption = wrap_plot_caption("Dashed lines: means across eight transition cantons. GR is contextual; Uri covers four DP municipalities.")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
        plot.caption.position = "plot",
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 11, lineheight = 1.1,
                                    margin = margin(t = 8))) # Legend below

eq1_scatter # Print plot
```

@fig-district-magnitude shows no clear, consistent relationship between historical district structure and smaller parties' mean seat-share gains across the eight transition cantons. For mean district magnitude, the group difference is opposite to the expected direction. For the share of districts below nine seats, it is consistent with the expectation but sensitive to Schaffhausen’s inclusion. The numerical comparisons below give each canton equal weight.

For the mean district magnitude, the average gains for the below mean group are `r sprintf("%.2f", eq1_groups$mean_gain_pp[eq1_groups$metric == "Mean district size (seats)" & eq1_groups$group == "Below mean"])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", eq1_groups$mean_gain_pp[eq1_groups$metric == "Mean district size (seats)" & eq1_groups$group == "At/above mean"])` percentage points for the at/above mean group. The at/above group results are relatively spread out, while the below-mean group's cantons are quite close to each other. The below-minus-above difference is `r sprintf("%+.2f", eq1_differences$below_minus_above_pp[eq1_differences$metric == "Mean district size (seats)"])` percentage points and with that opposite to the expected direction. 

For the share of districts below nine seats, the average gains for the below mean group are `r sprintf("%.2f", eq1_groups$mean_gain_pp[eq1_groups$metric == "Districts below 9 seats (%)" & eq1_groups$group == "Below mean"])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", eq1_groups$mean_gain_pp[eq1_groups$metric == "Districts below 9 seats (%)" & eq1_groups$group == "At/above mean"])` percentage points for the at/above mean group. The group gains of `r sprintf("%.2f", -eq1_differences$below_minus_above_pp[eq1_differences$metric == "Districts below 9 seats (%)"])` percentage points more are consistent with the expected direction. 

To analyze the sensitivity of the results to certain cantons, a leave one canton out check was carried out. The check showed that the results in exploratory question 1 are sensitive to the omission of the canton of Schaffhausen. The omission of Schaffhausen, lets the mean difference change from -3.06 to -1.06. For the share below 9 seats measure the direction switches with the omission of the canton. This means that without the canton of Schaffhausen, the average gains for the below mean groups are higher than for the above mean group, which oposses the estimated direction. Generally there is substantial variation in both groups, which means that also the omission of cantons like Uri and Valais has substantial impact on some of the measures. The exact results to the robustness checks can be found in @sec-leave-one-out.

Taken together, the two district measures reveal no consistent pattern linking the initial district structure to smaller parties' gains. This is combined with substantial variation within the analyzed groups. Further are the two measures sensitive to the omission of single cantons. The sensitivity supports the assessment of a missing pattern. The sensitivity to Schaffhausen can be linked to its comparatively high seat-share gain and possibly to the priorly discussed separate classification of affiliated lists as smaller parties. These descriptive comparisons therefore can not show any causal effect of the district magnitude.

#### Exploratory question 2: Explicit electoral quorums {#sec-eq2}

Exploratory question 2 researches on whether the implementation of explicit electoral quroums has an influence on the smaller parties seat-share gain. The explicit quorums ensure that only parties which reach a specific vote-share are considered for the allocation of seats. This may prevent smaller parties' from entering the parliament, which is why it's expected that in cantons with a quorum, the seat-share gain of smaller parties is reduced.

As documented in the @tbl-dp-adoption, have five out of eight analysis cantons applied a threshold. Of these five cantons, Aargau is a special case, since the canton applied it only after their first election under Double Pukelsheim. The most often used explicit quorum is the combination of a 5% district-level and a 3% cantonal level threshold of which at least one has to be reached. This combination was used in 9 of 19 elections held with an explicit threshold. 

The difference is visualized followingly as two grouped dot plots.
```{r}
#| label: fig-quorums
#| fig-cap: "Smaller-party seat-share gains by explicit electoral quorum."
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8.3
#| echo: false
eq2_elections <- small_party_summary |>
  mutate(
    canton = str_sub(election_id, 1, 2), # Extract canton code
    election_year = 2000L + as.integer(str_sub(election_id, 4, 5)), # Convert id to to full year
    quorum = case_when(
      election_id == "AG_09" ~ "Without explicit quorum", # Aargau had no quorum in 2009
      canton %in% c("NW", "SH", "UR") ~ "Without explicit quorum",
      canton %in% c("AG", "GR", "SZ", "VS", "ZG", "ZH") ~ "With explicit quorum",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    quorum = factor(
      quorum,
      levels = c("Without explicit quorum", "With explicit quorum")
    ),
    threshold = case_when( # Distinguish thresholds within the explicit-quorum group
      canton == "GR" ~ "GR (context only)",
      quorum == "Without explicit quorum" ~ "Without explicit quorum",
      canton == "ZH" & between(election_year, 2007, 2019) ~ # Zurich, changed quroum after 2019
        "5% district-level",
      (canton == "ZH" & election_year == 2023) | 
        (canton == "AG" & election_year >= 2012) |
        (canton == "ZG" & election_year >= 2014) ~
        "5% district or 3% cantonal",
      canton == "SZ" & election_year >= 2016 ~
        "1% cantonal",
      canton == "VS" & election_year >= 2017 ~
        "8% sub-district-level",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

stopifnot(
  !anyNA(eq2_elections$quorum),
  !anyNA(eq2_elections$threshold)
) # Check that every election has a quorum category and threshold label

eq2_cantons <- eq2_elections |>
  filter(canton != "GR") |> # Exclude GR from group means
  group_by(quorum) |>
  summarise(
    cantons = n_distinct(canton),
    elections = n(),
    mean_gain_pp = mean(seat_gain_pp), # Weight each election equally
    .groups = "drop"
  )

eq2_groups <- eq2_cantons |>
  select(quorum, mean_gain_pp) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = quorum, values_from = mean_gain_pp) |>
  mutate(
    without_minus_with_pp =
      `Without explicit quorum` - `With explicit quorum`
  ) # Calculate the difference between group means

threshold_colours <- c( # give each threshold group a different colour
  "Without explicit quorum"   = "#0072B2", 
  "1% cantonal"               = "#6e5d47", 
  "5% district-level"         = "#f8a765", 
  "5% district or 3% cantonal" = "#f06508", 
  "8% sub-district-level"     = "#883705", 
  "GR (context only)"         = "#8A8A8A"  
)
# Duplicate the observations for the two sample comparisons
eq2_plot_data <- bind_rows(
  eq2_elections |>
    mutate(sample = "Full sample"),

  eq2_elections |>
    filter(canton != "SH") |>
    mutate(sample = "Excluding Schaffhausen")
) |>
  mutate(
    sample = factor(
      sample,
      levels = c("Full sample", "Excluding Schaffhausen")
    )
  )

# Calculate the group means separately within each sample.
# GR remains visible but is excluded from all means.
eq2_plot_means <- eq2_plot_data |>
  filter(canton != "GR") |>
  group_by(sample, quorum) |>
  summarise(
    mean_gain_pp = mean(seat_gain_pp),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Calculate the left-to-right mean difference: with quorum minus without quorum.
eq2_plot_differences <- eq2_plot_means |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = quorum,
    values_from = mean_gain_pp
  ) |>
  mutate(
    difference_pp =
      `With explicit quorum` - `Without explicit quorum`
  )

# Place all visible labels in one repel layer so they avoid each other.
# Empty labels make the mean diamonds obstacles without adding more text.
eq2_label_data <- bind_rows(
    eq2_plot_data |>
    transmute(
      sample,
      label_x = as.numeric(quorum),
      seat_gain_pp,
      plot_label = if_else( # label only schaffhausen elections
        canton == "SH" & sample == "Full sample",
        election_id,
        ""
      ),
      label_colour = threshold,
      label_face = "plain",
      label_size = 3
    ),
  eq2_plot_differences |>
    transmute(
      sample, label_x = 1.5,
      seat_gain_pp = (`Without explicit quorum` + `With explicit quorum`) / 2,
      plot_label = sprintf("%+.2f pp", difference_pp),
      label_colour = "Mean difference", label_face = "bold", label_size = 3.5
    ),
  eq2_plot_means |>
    transmute(
      sample, label_x = as.numeric(quorum), seat_gain_pp = mean_gain_pp,
      plot_label = "", label_colour = "Mean difference",
      label_face = "plain", label_size = 3
    ),
  # Unlabelled points along each arrow keep text away from the connector.
  eq2_plot_differences |>
    group_by(sample) |>
    reframe(
      label_x = seq(1, 2, length.out = 25),
      seat_gain_pp = seq(
        first(`Without explicit quorum`), first(`With explicit quorum`),
        length.out = 25
      ),
      plot_label = "", label_colour = "Mean difference",
      label_face = "plain", label_size = 3
    )
)

eq2_group_plot <- ggplot(
  eq2_plot_data,
  aes(quorum, seat_gain_pp, colour = threshold) # Group on x-axis, threshold determines colour
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70", linewidth = .35) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = eq2_label_data,
    aes(
      x = label_x, y = seat_gain_pp, label = plot_label,
      colour = label_colour, fontface = label_face, size = I(label_size)
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    seed = 1,
    nudge_y = .3,
    direction = "both",
    box.padding = .35,
    point.padding = .25,
    force = 3,
    force_pull = .3,
    max.time = Inf,
    max.iter = 100000,
    segment.colour = "grey65",
    segment.size = .25,
    max.overlaps = Inf,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  # Connect the two group means within each panel.
geom_segment(
  data = eq2_plot_differences,
  aes(
    x = 1,
    xend = 2,
    y = `Without explicit quorum`,
    yend = `With explicit quorum`
  ),
  inherit.aes = FALSE,
  colour = "grey40",
  linewidth = 0.6,
  arrow = grid::arrow(
    ends = "last",
    type = "closed",
    length = grid::unit(2, "mm")
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    data = eq2_plot_means,
    aes(quorum, mean_gain_pp),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, # Group means do not have a threshold category
    shape = 18,
    size = 5,
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
  vars(sample),
  nrow = 1,
  scales = "fixed", # giving both panels the same y-axis
) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(threshold_colours, "Mean difference" = "black"),
    breaks = names(threshold_colours) # Set legend order
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
  labels = c(
    "Without explicit quorum" = "Without explicit\nquorum",
    "With explicit quorum" = "With explicit\nquorum"
  )
) +
  labs( # Label the plot
    x = NULL,
    y = "Aggregate smaller-party seat-share gain (pp)",
    colour = "Electoral threshold",
    caption = wrap_plot_caption(
      "Black diamonds: equally weighted election means, excluding GR.",
      "Arrows connect group means from left to right.",
      "Labels: mean with quorum minus mean without quorum (pp)."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(
      size=13,
      face ="bold",
      margin = margin(b=8)
    ),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 11, lineheight = 1.1,
                                margin = margin(t = 8))
  ) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)) # Arrange legend in two columns

eq2_group_plot # Display the plot
```

@fig-quorums provides a descriptive comparison of smaller-party seat-share gains by the presence of an explicit electoral quorum. Average gains are higher in the group without an explicit quorum with `r sprintf("%.1f", eq2_cantons$mean_gain_pp[eq2_cantons$quorum == "Without explicit quorum"])` percentage points than in the group with one and `r sprintf("%.1f", eq2_cantons$mean_gain_pp[eq2_cantons$quorum == "With explicit quorum"])` percentage points. Both groups exhibit substantial variation. As priorly mentioned, is the canton of Schaffhausen sticking out. 

Especially interesting, is the case of the canton Aargau, where in 2009 the election was held without a threshold and in the elections 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024 with a threshold. The data shows that the seat-share gain for the pre-reform election 2009 and the first post-reform election 2012 is equally big with 9.3 percentage points. In the subsequent elections, though the seat-share gain dropped accordingly to the assumption. While the unchanged gain between 2009 and 2012 contrasts with the assumption, the subsequent elections are in line with it. For Aargau there is therefore no clear pattern visible, moreover, the seat-share gain difference might be influenced by further unobserved circumstances. 

To analyze whether the effect holds despite the variation, the leave one canton out sensitivity check was performed. As priorly is the high seat-share gain of Schaffhausen making the analysis and the results sensitive to the omission of it. Schaffhausen accounts for five of the twelve elections in the group without an explicit quorum, with all five having seat-share gains above the group average. With Schaffhausen's exclusion the difference flips from a 3.56 pp higher gain for the without quroum group to a by 0.67 pp smaller gain. That means without Schaffhausen, the observed effect is not aligned anymore with the stated expectation. The exact results for the omission of every canton are outlined in @sec-leave-one-out.

To summarize the analysis about the effect of the implementation of explicit quoroms, it can be stated that within the 31 relevant election a difference which matches the expectation can be seen. This difference though is sensitive to the inclusion of Schaffhausen. Furthermore, the limited amount of elections held till date and the different application of thresholds and electoral law, encourage to interpret the difference with caution.

#### Exploratory question 3: Change across successive elections

The preceding analysis showed that cantons differ in their implementation of the Double Pukelsheim system. These institutional differences motivate a closer examination of within-canton patterns. The last exploratory question therefore examines how the smaller parties' seat-share gains changed across successive elections within a canton. For that each canton and its successive changes are analyzed separately. To possibly better understand changes, events such as electoral reforms and changes in the party composition are documented. Generally stable positive values of $\Delta_e$ indicate a persistent mechanical advantage for smaller parties, while substantial fluctuation or even changes in sign would suggest that the effect is strongly dependent on the individual circumstances of an election. 

Since @fig-successive-elections aligns every Double Pukelsheim election for each canton independently by their order, the first election under the system is numbered 1, the next is numbered 2, and so on. This means that the same election number represents different calendar years across cantons.  The same measures as in the main hypothesis are taken, to calculate the seat-share differences. The smaller-party category is recalculated for each election using the existing vote-share cutoff of less than 10%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-successive-elections

# Reuse the election-level outcome calculated from the main Hypothesis.

eq3_elections <- small_party_summary |>

stopifnot(

stopifnot(

eq3_plot <- ggplot(
```

```{r}
#| label: eq3-summary
#| include: false

# Calculate average transition changes and average seat-share gain by election number
eq3_election_stats <- eq3_elections |>
  filter(!is_graubuenden) |> # Exclude Graubünden 
  arrange(canton, election_number) |> # Order elections chronologically for each canton
  group_by(canton) |> # Calculate changes separately for each canton.
  mutate(
    change_pp = seat_gain_pp - lag(seat_gain_pp) # calculate difference between preceeding and current election
  ) |>
  ungroup() |> # remove canton grouping for 2nd calculation
  group_by(election_number) |> # Group 1st, 2nd, 3rd etc elections together
  summarise(
    cantons = n_distinct(canton), # Count cantons for each group
    mean_gain_pp = mean(seat_gain_pp), # Calculate the equally weighted average seat-share gain.
    mean_change_pp = if (all(is.na(change_pp))) {
      NA_real_ # Election 0 doesn't exist, therefore excluded later in the note
    } else {
      mean(change_pp, na.rm = TRUE) # Average the within-canton changes, excluding missing values.
    },
    .groups = "drop" 
  ) |>
  arrange(election_number) # Display the results
```

::: {.callout-note title="EQ3 summary"} 
The average within-canton change in smaller parties' seat-share gain was `r with(filter(eq3_election_stats, election_number > 1L), paste(sprintf("%+.1f pp from election %d to %d (%d cantons)", mean_change_pp, election_number - 1L, election_number, cantons), collapse = "; "))`. The average seat-share gains across the cantons were `r paste(sprintf("%.1f pp in election %d (%d cantons)", eq3_election_stats$mean_gain_pp, eq3_election_stats$election_number, eq3_election_stats$cantons), collapse = "; ")`. For each transition, the average gives equal weight to all cantons observed in both elections. Graubünden is excluded.
:::

Generally speaking, the seat-share gains with some canton-specific fluctuations, are relatively persistent. As seen in the analysis of Hypothesis 1, there is with Uri 2020 only one election, in which no positive seat-share gain was seen. This is the case, since there no *smaller_party* ran. Another interesting observation, is the fact that the average seat-share gain rises successively from election to election. Despite the seen effect is the number of cantons limited and further lowers throughout the later elections. For a possible effect speaking is, that the cantons of Schaffhausen and Zurich which appear in all comparisons and have relatively high seat-gain shares also experience drops in their share throughout the elections. These dropps occurr, while the average seat-share gain rises continuously. Additionally, the analysis is less dependent on political trends specific to a single election year, since for example the second elections held under Double Pukelsheim range from 2011 in Zurich to 2024 in Uri. The range though does not isolate the pattern from political trends. A possible partial explanation for the observed pattern, is the broader increase in party-system fragmentation, which was documented by Lüscher (2024, pp. 133-135). This because if smaller parties receive wider support, their combined disadvantage under the former Hagenbach-Bischoff and with that their seat-share gain under Double Pukelsheim may increase. Nevertheless, whether this mechanism actually explains the observed pattern remains untested.

Besides the broader image, there are also interesting patterns within the cantons. The biggest changes between two elections, can be seen for Schaffhausen, Zurich and Nidwalden. In Schaffhausen the seat-share gain rose from the first to the 2nd election from roughly 10 to roughly 17 percentage points, where it settled afterward quite stably. A possible partial reason, is the higher number of smaller parties in the parliament which increased from seven in 2008 to nine in 2012. From the 2015 Zurich, to the 2019 Zurich election, the seat-share gain dropped by roughly 5 percentage points, a reason for this is possibly, that both the GLP and the Greens exceeded the 10% smaller-parties threshold while the BDP lost its parliamentary representation. This led to the circumstance, that from seven smaller parliamentary parties in 2015, the number dropped to four in 2019. In Nidwalden since the implementation the seat-gain share rose continuously. The strongest difference  was observed from the 3rd to the 4th election, where the share rose by 5 percentage points. This effect might be partially influenced by the smaller party composition, since the green party fell below the 10% threshold.  For Aargau, Zug, Schwyz and Valais we can observe relatively stable patterns with smaller fluctuations. The canton of Valais, records relatively low seat-share gains  across the three elections. This pattern is consistent with the possibility, that the restricted pooling, has a limiting effect. Nevertheless this analysis is not isolating this feature and a potential effect. For the canton of Uri only two elections were observed, which is why no pattern can be inferred.

In the two cantons Aargau and Zurich, the Double Pukelsheim system, was adjusted after its implementation. In Aargau in 2012, a threshold was introduced, detailed information can be found in @sec-eq2. The assumption of the implementation of a threshold is that the smaller-party seat share gain declines with it. The post electoral change results for the canton of Aargau don't present a clear picture. There are results in accordance as also speaking against the assumption. The absence of a clear effect, may be partly explained through that in each election the biggest list without parliamentary representation, received only between 0.1% and 0.7% vote shares.^[For cantonal vote shares and parliamentary representation, see T. Schaub (2012, p. 12), Staatskanzlei des Kantons Aargau (2016b, p. 2), Staatskanzlei des Kantons Aargau (2020, p. 2), and Staatskanzlei des Kantons Aargau (2024).] This suggests that the explicit quorums in Aargau only had limited scope to exclude parties, which otherwise would have won seats. In the canton of Zurich, in the year 2023 a quorum change applied. To the existing 5% district-level quorum an alternative 3% canton-wide threshold was added. This electoral change is in the tendency increasing the seat-share gain, since it possibly enables more parties to reach the seat-allocation process. In the 2023 election, though no party profited from this clause, since every qualifying party also reached the 5% district-level threshold (Regierungsrat des Kantons Zürich, 2023, p.9). Further, the seat-share gain dropped from the 2019 to the 2023 election. Overall, the two electoral changes therefore had no visible direct effect on the smaller party seat-share gain.

To check for robustness and sensitivity, the leave one canton out check was performed. The check was done for each election number separately. Throughout all checks does the seat-share gain remains positive. The mean change though from election three to four and from four to five switches signs when Zurich, respectively the canton of Aargau is excluded. These later transitions include only five respectively three cantons and are therefore more sensitive to individual cantons. The exact statistics for the robustness check can be found in @sec-leave-one-out.

The analysis across all 31 elections, therefore indicates that the mechanical seat-share gain for smaller parties persists across successive elections. The strength and variation in the magnitude differ between the cantons. In the analyzed elections, the gain not only persisted, but rose across sucessive elections. The average within-canton change though isn't rising consecutively with a small decline between the third and fourth election. Moreover, the analysis is sensitive for the within-canton change to the omission of single cantons. The analysis and its effects may be partly affected through the changes in the party composition of the smaller-party group. The results therefore imply a consistent gain for smaller-parties across cantons and elections. However it can't be established and is not inferred or mentioned by the literature, that additional elections under Double Pukelsheim increase the gain.

## Discussion

In this paper, the general question: "20 Years of the Double Pukelsheim System in Switzerland: What Is the Mechanical Effect of the Transition from the Hagenbach-Bischoff Method on the Seat Distribution of Smaller Parties? " was answered in two parts. In the first step, the mechanical effect on the smaller parties was examined. Subsequently the study examined which conditions could lead to differences in the strength of the mechanical effect across cantons or elections. 

Regarding the first step, it was found that across elections the smaller parties collectively gain seat shares under Double Pukelsheim compared to Hagenbach Bischoff. The average aggregate unweighted seat-share gain was 7.6 percentage points. Further in 30 of the 31 analyzed elections, the smaller parties aggregately received a higher seat-share. In the Uri 2020 election, no eligible smaller party contested, thus no seat-share difference could be observed. The gain also persisted when adapting the 10% smaller parties threshold to 8% and 12%, and after the exclusion of any single canton. Further it was observed that most smaller parties also individually profited from the transition. The findings in Hypothesis 1 are consistent with the idea of the upper apportionment process, that it lowers the share of ineffective votes and with that increases the equality of electoral success. (Lüscher, 2024, p. 3)

This finding further matches the observations of the existing literature. Leuzinger states that in his analysis across seven elections, smaller parties generally received more seats under the new system (Leuzinger, 2018, p.42) Also in the Zurich 2011 election by Pukelsheim and Schuhmacher and in the Schwyz 2016 election analyzed by Lüscher, smaller parties profited from the implementation (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011 ; Lüscher , 2024, p.13). 

In the second step, it was examined, whether the effect varied based on the different circumstances of the cantons. First it was analyzed with two measures whether the pre-reform district sizes have an impact on the seat-share gain or not. No consistent relationship between the prior constituency sizes and the gain for smaller parties was found. This is contrary to the formulated expectation. This expectation was, that in cantons with smaller pre-reform districts, where the high natural thresholds impose a greater disadvantage, the upper apportionment and its cantonwide mechanism would have a greater effect. The expectation, was also based on Lüscher's finding that in cantons which priorly had smaller districts, the proportionality had increased more strongly (Lüscher, 2024, pp.132-133). The lack of evidence in this analysis does not contradict Lüscher's findings, since an improvement in overall proportionality doesn't need to have a direct impact on the seat-share gain for smaller parties.

A second exploratory question, examined whether there is a difference in the mechanical seat-share gain between elections held with and without an explicit quoroum. The examination here observed a higher seat-share gain for cantons without an explicit quroum. This fits the literature, since Lüscher and the Federal State Chancellery, both argue that explicit thresholds can restrict the gains among smaller parties. This since thresholds may partly offset the greater proportionality achieved through the upper apportionment (Bundeskanzlei, 2013, p. 18; Lüscher, 2024, pp. 107, 135). Thus of the seen effect in the analysis and the support of the theory for an effect, is the effect seen in this analysis sensitive to the inclusion of Schaffhausen. The sensitivity goes to a point, that without the Schaffhausen elections, the effect reverses. Therefore the observed effect needs to be interpreted cautiously.

The third exploratory question analyzes the seat-share gains across successive elections within and with respect to each cantons' electoral rules. Through this approach, it brings together elements of the preceding analyses. The results show that the positive seat-share advantage generally persists across successive elections, further supporting the main finding. Although average gains are higher at later election numbers, mean within-canton changes do not follow a consistently increasing pattern. Moreover, fewer cantons contribute to the later comparisons, and some changes are sensitive to the inclusion of individual cantons. The findings therefore do not establish that additional elections under Double Pukelsheim increase smaller parties' mechanical seat-share gain.

In order to analyze all relevant elections and their various underlying assumptions, a few assumptions had to be made. The analysis, holds all post-reform votes constant and identifies the conditional mechanical difference, without capturing the behavioural effect of the transition. For the cantons in which priorly list alliances were allowed, no hypothetical list alliances are formed in this thesis. This decision might in the relevant cantons understate the smaller lists representation under the Hagenbach-Bischoff counterfactual. Further, each list, which ran independently, was treated as a separate party, since the Double Pukelsheim algorithm also treats them separately. This decision is especially relevant in Schaffhausen, where across multiple elections, several affiliated lists such as Youth or special-interest lists ran. In addition to these decisions, the limited number of cantons and their different electoral laws, limit the extent to which the observed differences in gains can be attributed to a single feature. 

For cantons considering a transition from Hagenbach–Bischoff to Double Pukelsheim, the following can be stated. With 30 of the 31 analyzed elections showing a collective seat-share gain for smaller parties, the findings suggest that a similar mechanical advantage would arise in other cantons adopting DP. However, its magnitude depends on canton-specific circumstances, such as electoral rules, district sizes, and vote distributions. Behavioural responses by parties and voters introduce further uncertainty. It therefore makes sense for cantons to calculate a hypothetical DP allocation based on their observed Hagenbach–Bischoff election results. This allows them to assess the potential mechanical seat-share changes while explicitly accounting for their electoral structure and the proposed DP rules. 

Further research could extend this thesis in the following ways: With examining how plausible counterfactual list-alliances affect the estimated gains. As also with addressing the explicit quoroums and their possible effects. Specifically it could recalculate each observed election under different electoral quroums, ceteris paribus, to isolate their mechanical effect on smaller parties' representation. 

## Conclusion

In this paper, I examined the mechanical effect of the transition from the Hagenbach-Bischoff Method to the Double Pukelsheim on the seat distribution of smaller parties. The thesis focused on examining the seat-share differences between the two systems, for parties with less than 10% vote share. For this all 31 elections held by the eight transition cantons from HB to DP were analyzed, while holding all votes constant. 

For all held elections, the average unweighted seat-share gain was 7.6 percentage points for the aggregate smaller parties group. In 30 of 31 elections, the smaller parties collectively gained seat-shares. The Uri 2020 election is the exception, where no list below the 10% smaller parties threshold contested. The result of a positive seat-share difference, further persisted with alternative cutoffs for the smaller-parties group and when excluding individual cantons. These findings therefore descriptively support Hypothesis 1. 

The further analysis, explored potential differences between cantons, based on pre-reform district sizes and explicit quorums. For the relationship between the pre-reform district sizes and the seat-share gain, no consistent pattern could be observed. Regarding differences between elections held with and without a quroum, a higher seat-share gain for elections without a quroum was observed. However, the observed difference is sensitive to individual cantons. Further it was found, that average gains persisted and even increased across successive election numbers, even when individual cantons were excluded. However the average within-canton changes were less consistent and sensitive to canton exclusions. This pattern doesn't establish that additional elections under Double Pukelsheim increase the seat-share gain.

However, this analysis is only focusing on mechanical differences conditional on the canton specific rules and on the observed post-reform votes and not estimating the reform's complete effect. This paper extends the existing knowledge about the mechanical seat-share gains for smaller parties by covering all 31 available elections for the eight transition cantons, including the successive elections within each canton. This enables a wider basis to assess the magnitude and consistency of the smaller parties' advantage under the Double Pukelsheim.
